utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, will you handle the next witness -- not handle the next witness, will you question the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The Prosecution will call Colonel Ludwik Kranjc. COLONEL LUDWIK KRANJC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you take that oath, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Colonel Kranjc, would you state for the record your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Ludwik Kranjc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you born in Slovenia in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on September 13 in 1943 in the municipality of Lasko, Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After your primary schooling did you attend the Yugoslav Military Academy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Military Academy in Belgrade I was from 1962 to 1965.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was one of the class mates in your graduating class?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the sublieutenants who graduated with me in 1965 was today's General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was your area of military expertise during your service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My speciality was officer of armoured and mechanized units of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did your service with the military end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My military service ended on October 31st 1962 (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was your rank when your service ended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My rank was Colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Colonel Kranjc, the translation of the answer to the question of when did your service end says October 31st 1962. Did you mean to say 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, I am sorry. My military service ended on October 31st 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From what army was your separation effected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served in the Yugoslav People's Army and I officially completed my service in the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At the time you left the military, what was the position that you were working at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the army I completed my military service serving as Operations Officer in the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was that Corps headquartered in the Banja Luka region of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that Corps was headquartered in the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Between September 1965 and September of 1992, can you briefly describe what types of commands and other major positions you held in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1965 until 1971 I held various lower command posts in the Educational Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you command armoured units at the Company, Battalion and Brigade level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then from 1971 until 1972 I was Operations Officer in the Commander of the regiments in Slovenia and then Commander of Battalion in Vipava until 1975. Then I went to the Command Staff Academy which I graduated in 1977 with excellent marks. Then from 1977 until 1982, I was head of a course in the Military Academy in the Educational Centre in Banja Luka. Then I was transferred to Belgrade to Chief of Staff of the 1st Mechanized Corps until 1984. From 1984 until 1985 I completed the school for National Defence -- the highest educational institution in the Yugoslav People's Army. From 1985 until 1989 I was Commander of a Mechanized Brigade in Pancevo. Then I was transferred to Banja Luka, and from 1989 until 1991 I was Operations Officer in the command of the mentioned 5th Corps. From May 1991 until May 1992, I was Commander of the Educational Centre for armoured and mechanized units in Banja Luka and in May I was transferred to the command of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The designator of the 5th Corps was later changed to the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May or end of May, the name the 5th Corps of the 2nd Military District was renamed the 1st Krajina Corps of the army of the Republic -- I am sorry, of the army of the Republika Srspka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During your training as a junior officer and at the various military academies you attended, were you taught that there was a standard method and format for preparing an operations order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Military Academy we were taught operational tasks up to the level of the battalion, and in the Academy planning and conduct of operations up to the level of army and Corps, and in the National Army School, in addition to planning for the Corps and army command, also planning the use of the total armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the format, the basic format, for an operations order consistent throughout your entire career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The planning of combat operations was regulated by combat regulations for a certain level of unit and by certain other regulations and hand books which were applicable to the whole armed forces. Those rules were respected throughout my service in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were all officers involved in planning in every unit in the JNA required to follow the format?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They participated as regulated by their posts. There were definite instructions. At the lower level, the officers knew how to use and come and plan combat operations for their level, and high level officers were familiar with the rules at the higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain the process and the content of a combat operations order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When a unit Commander is given a task from his superior command, he studies the task to understand it and has a basic concept about it which he conveys to the members of his command; and then command bodies, according to their competencies and the departments for which they are responsible, prepare proposals to the Commander for the use and commitment of units. After those proposals, the unit Commander passes the main decision and familiarises the command members with it. On the basis of that, the final order is issued for combat commitment of units. This order consists of several parts or points. The order begins with data on the enemy or the aggressor or opponent. Then in the second point the task of that particular unit which is being committed is defined. In the third point, the tasks and data about neighbouring units of one's own forces, right and left, forward and behind, if there are such units. In the fourth point, the decision is expressed, briefly described, the decision of the Commander which says in which way the Commander with subordinated units will carry out the task specified in point two. In point five and the subitems of that point, the specific tasks are indicated for the use of units, including the direction in which they should act or the zone for which they are responsible, the way in which they should execute those tasks, who will support them, where is the command post of that unit, and some other necessary data. In the following points the artillery engineers, anti-aircraft and other types of support for units are described. Then comes a point talking about logistics support, then a point about moral support, intelligence, political and others. Finally, the order ends with the command structure and signals, where is the command post of the unit and in which way communication will be achieved among units; and after that the Commander signs the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Does the order have to be signed by the Commander of the unit preparing it before it is released to the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it has to be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Assuming that time permits before action is required, does each order for offensive combat operations have to be approved by a higher headquarters before execution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So, in the instant that a Brigade is the originating unit for the order, that would mean that it would have to be submitted to the Corps for approval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Brigade command or, rather, the Brigade acts according to orders received from the Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Likewise, for Corps it would have to submit its orders for offensive combat actions to the main staff of the General Staff for approval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Corps command receives orders from its superior command. At the time of June, July and on, 1992, it was the command of the 1st Krajina Corps which received its commands from the main staff of the army of the Republika Srspka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In an instance where the Corps was initiating a combat operation on its own, would it have to notify the main staff of its order or plan for combat operations prior to its execution, assuming time permitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the units knew it. It applied to the Corps command and the obligations of the Corps command and the Commander. So the subordinate units knew their obligations on reporting, upon receiving orders and what to do upon receiving those orders from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was that process used in every unit that you were a member of during your career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, I am familiar with the chain of command between the Corps command and the main staff, and the Corps command and subordinate units. In those two levels, upward and downward, the chain of command was carried out in accordance with existing regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was this process and these procedures introduced and taught at the mechanized school centre in Banja Luka while you were the chief of the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that process was used and the young cadets, the future officers, were taught about the way in which that process was prepared and executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this document marked as the next Prosecution Exhibit? That would be 179. If that could be handed to the witness? (Exhibit 179 was handed to the witness) (To the witness): Colonel Kranjc, are you familiar with that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen that document, but I can read it and I can understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If that document could be placed on the elmo, please, the Serbian version first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the top it says, "Main staff of the army of the Republika Srspka. Strictly confidential. No. 02/2-109, date 28.08.1994. Very urgent". That is the established format. One has to place either a stamp or the inscription indicating the name of the unit or command or body sending the document, the level of confidentiality and the date, below that the level of urgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Colonel Kranjc, just generally what is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The substance of this document is that the main staff of the army of the Republika Srspka is ordering the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and the Eastern Bosnian Corps, and also the document is being sent to the command post of the main staff of the army of the Republika Srspka, and to the Fifth Kozara Light Infantry Brigade. It is ordering ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could just ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the commitment of a part of forces in an operation which the main staff has code named "breza-94". Later on, it specifies the obligations of the Eastern Bosnian Corps to carry out the transfer of units into full combat readiness and to prepare one Battalion and to send it within the 1st Krajina Corps. A deadline is given for that Battalion to report to the Operations region on 4th September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender the document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 179 will be admitted. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Colonel Kranjc, is that document representative of the standard type of order, general order, for an operation that the Corps would be given from the main staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but if I may, I would like to add in the terminology of the Yugoslav People's Army which has been taken over by the army of Yugoslavia and the army of the Republika Srpska, we distinguished two names of documents, "zapovjest" as broader combat document ordering the use of combat units in a major assignment, and "naredjenje" or order, instructions, which assign tasks of lesser magnitude and which lasted shorter; as in this case, this is a naredjenje, but there is also a zapovjest -- both words meaning "order" -- at a higher level and which is more detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What requirements does this document place on the 1st Corps and the Eastern Bosnian Corps -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Keegan, could you put the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to once the witness had gone through the version. He can read all the way through the document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first part of the order came from the main staff to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and the Eastern Bosnian Corps, and it was signed by Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic, and the other one by Lieutenant General Momir Talic. In that order, the command of the 6th Serbian Infantry Brigade and the 5th Kozara Infantry Brigade are ordered to report at a briefing of Commanders of those units, those performing tasks within the operation Breza-94, and to bring to the briefing decisions on the use of units and to be ready to explain the same as well as to elaborate on the method of implementation of that operation, the Breza-94 is implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could we have the English version, please? Colonel Kranjc, is this document a fair or good representation of the procedure for the development of combat orders which you described earlier, that is, specifically the direction from the higher unit for the development of a plan and then the requirement to report by the Commanders of how they intend to accomplish the basic tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we could call it a school example of the way in which an order is worded and conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Breza-94, was that an operation involving the employment of Serbian forces into the Bihac Velika Kladusa area, region, of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, that operation was to have been carried out from the region of the Republika Srspka west across the Una River to the region of the so-called western Autonomous province of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did it involve the movement of units through the territory that was known as the Republika Srspka Krajina, that is, Croatia territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Colonel Kranjc, you testified that it was required for orders of combat actions to be briefed to higher headquarters for approval where time permitted. Was it also the requirement for all unit Commanders to receive approval of their superior prior to committing their units to any offensive military actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So, for example, if the 343 Brigade or any of its units from Prijedor were going to be engaged in a military attack in the Prijedor Kozarac area, would Colonel Arsic have to have notified the command of the 1st Krajina Corps prior to that attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he should.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If time or other circumstances did not permit communication to the Corps prior to the military attack, would the Brigade Commander be responsible to notify the Corps as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he should in the most appropriate way, in the best way, as soon as possible he should notify them either through a liaison officer, through radio, by telephone means; that is, there were several possibilities in which one could inform the superior command about an action undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were on the staff of the 5th Corps and, as it was later known, the 1st Krajina Corps, was the commanding officer of the Corps, commanding General, aware of the details of the Corps' operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the reporting requirements for the units of the Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Subordinated units had to report or inform the Corps Commander in several ways when receiving lower level order that they had received this order, and that they had embarked on its implementation, that they had engaged in combat operations on the basis of the orders, how these combat operations are conducted and, finally, the outcome of the task performed. Furthermore, the combat regulations or instructions envisaged that daily combat reports needed to be filed, and such reports covered the information as follows, information about the enemy, the situation in the territory, the situation in the unit, the success level, execution of the task during the day, the decision or the ideas of the Commander of that particular unit about operations in the forthcoming period and requests and needs regarding further combat necessities addressed to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In addition to these daily reports, did the Brigade commanders also have direct private communication with the Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had to have it and they did have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the reporting requirements in the 1st Corps normally strictly enforced, that is, if a unit failed to meet its reporting requirements was the Corps staff responsible for determining what the problem was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The units complied with this reporting order very strictly, by and large; in case a unit did not, could not, failed to do so, to submit a report for whatever reason, then depending on the importance of that unit, the operations body of the Corps command intervened immediately with the operations body of that unit, and from time to time with the Commander directly why the report had not been sent and requested information, even if very briefly, even if very brief, either over the telephone or through other means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During 1992 do you believe a situation could have existed in the 1st Corps where a Brigade engaged in offensive military attacks in the Banja Luka region using artillery, tanks and infantry troops and failed to notify the Corps Commander prior to the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the 343 Brigade under standing orders from the Corps when you arrived on the staff in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to the Chief of Staff of the Corps, 343 Brigade received orders from the Corps command in writing and in other forms in this identically as all other units of that Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there a language in those orders that reflected the prior standing orders that had been given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the orders that you saw given to the 343 Brigade begin with a reference to prior standing orders for its operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we sent orders about combat operations to the units for the 343 Brigade, the order usually said that it had to carry out its tasks according to the former, that is, original plan. The original plan I never saw in the documents that I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Under the defence structure of the former Yugoslavia, is it true that all TO units as well as police forces fell under the operational control of the JNA for military actions whenever a war or a state of emergency was declared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did that same organisational structure and requirements continue in the territory that was later known as the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Accordingly then, would the commanding General of a Corps or his principal Staff Officer have the authority and ability to control the military actions of any police or TO force that were within the Corps's zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he could discontinue the behaviour, the conduct, of these units or approve them, rather, give his consent to such behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a paramilitary group known as the Serbian Defence Forces or SOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was that group formed in the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was formed in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did members of that unit wear red berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the other name, either "Red Berets" or Serb Defence Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where was that unit trained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That group was trained at the military training grounds of the Educational Centre of the armoured and mechanized units called Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it because the Commander of the training grounds at Manjaca and my subordinate reported to me that in a facility next to a fish pond a group of uniformed individuals undergoing training for under water tank use, and that they were undergoing combat training for combat, and that the training at the grounds was authorised by my Assistant for Logistics, Colonel Subotic. When I learnt that, I called Colonel Subotic, my Logistics Assistant, and he confirmed that he had approved the use of this facility and the use of that area for the training. Then I reported, as appropriate, my superior, General Arandjelovic, Chief of the Administration of armoured and mechanized units in Belgrade who said, who approved it, and said that it could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What time frame was this that this training was going on in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the exact date, but I think it was February or March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What position did Lieutenant Colonel Subotic later go on to in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May 1992 he became the first Minister of Defence in the government of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Under the rules that you have described earlier, before this group, the SOS or Red Berets would be used for any significant military type action in the area of the 1st Krajina Corps, would the persons committing them to that action have to have notified the Commander of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if they were to be committed to a combat action, the Corps Commander would have to be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he is responsible for all combat operations in his area of responsibility because a Corps Commander is responsible for all military or combat operations in the area of responsibility of his Corps; and also since he knew about those forces, perhaps he envisaged the deployment of these forces otherwise, and if somebody else had already deployed them or committed them to something, then he would not be able to do that. He had to know where these forces were, whether they were free or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the Commander of the 1st Corps a member of the Krizni Stab in the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the Stab ex-officio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Which political group controlled the Krizni Stab in the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Party, the Serb Democratic Party, SDS, as they called them, controlled not only the operations of the Crisis Staff, but all the walks of life in the region of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there close co-operation between the Krizni Stab and the 1st Krajina Corps in the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was close co-operation, not only because the Commander or his Deputy was a member of the Crisis Staff and attending regular meetings, but there were also other contacts and close co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the organised military or paramilitary groups supported or organised by the SDS included within the armed forces utilized by the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Beginning with your tour of the 5th Corps (as it was then known) of the JNA in 1989 and continuing on through your time in Banja Luka in your final duties with the 1st Krajina Corps, had you ever seen any real intelligence information or evidence showing any preparation for jihad by Muslim groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During that same -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Keegan, what does that mean, "jihad"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Holy war. (To the witness): During that same time frame did you ever see any real military intelligence or evidence of any large scale arming or preparation for military operations by Muslim groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither did I see such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the Serbian population in the Banja Luka region armed by the JNA during 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it because I noticed and heard and saw that Colonel Subotic, my Logistics Assistant, with several other officers left the Educational Centre from time to time and was engaged in the transfer of weapons from various army depots to the area of Banja Luka and that it was then distributed at different points. He also talked to me about that, not in much detail, but that he was carrying out the tasks with which his superiors -- which his superiors knew about and that he was doing it for the sake of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What kind of scale are we talking about regarding the supply of these weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As it happened several times, and as he told me that he was going with several superiors, three or four, sometimes a dozen, that there was an officer in every vehicle. They did not use army vehicles for the transport, but larger trailer trucks of civilian organisations, and I think there were 10 or perhaps more such actions. I should say that about 10,000 -- it may be more -- of light weapons and other materiel and munition were transported, were brought, into the area in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that Lieutenant Colonel Subotic indicated his superiors knew what he was doing. Did he mention any superior by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He mentioned by name Major General Dragoljub Arandjelovic, head of the administration of armoured mechanized units in the General Staff of the JNA. In a conversation when I was reporting about General -- reporting to General Arandjelovic about the situation in the Educational Centre, he asked me what Colonel Subotic was doing and where he was. I notified him that he was carrying out the tasks that he himself knew about and he said, "Right, let him be."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What significant operations occurred while you were a part of the Operations staff at the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in the Operational staff of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, we planned some operations and the following were carried out: the withdrawal of the forces of the 1st Krajina Corps which had previously and until the end of June '92 deployed north of the Sava River in what is called West Slavonia. At the same time, we planned an operation to open the Sava valley corridor. Both operations were ordered by the main staff of the army of the Republika Srpska. Both operations were planned. One referred to the pull out of the forces from across the Sava and the second one, the opening corridor; and both were planned and carried out in conformity with existing regulations and the instructions of the main staff, the command staff. A third operation was also planned. That was the attack, an attempt to take Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did the fighting go in the Posavina corridor operation in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early June during the fighting for the opening of the Sava Valley corridor -- we called it "corridor" only -- a smaller number of units was committed in this operation, and there were the units of the so-called Doboj operations group, 327 Motorized Brigade in the area of Derventa, and around 10th June or a little later a Battalion was brought to reinforce it from the Serb Republic Krajina, from Knin, headed by Milan Martic. When the units of the 1st Corps were pulled out from across the Sava, that is, moved from the area West Slavonia to the territory of Republika Srpska, the units responsible for the opening of corridor were reinforced, and a larger part of the 1st Krajina Corps units was relocated there, such as the 6th Motorized Brigade, the 5th Kozara Brigade, the major part of the 329 (renamed later the 1st Armoured Brigade) and Light Brigades of the municipalities, from the territories centering around the corridor were also committed to it, Prnjavor, from Prnjavor, Srbac, Orsin, Kurnin(?), Trebava, and some other Light Brigades of the ARS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Several of those units you have just named, such as the 5th Kozara Brigade and the Light Brigade and the municipalities, had those previously been TO units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were TO units, except they were not Brigade, they were -- some were Detachments, some were Battalions of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At some point was the TO designation dropped and were they considered to be regular units of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not see such orders from the main staff, but I know that in June it was not possible to use the term "Territorial Defence" or simply went out of use. The "Territorial Defence unit" was not used any more. We used the term "Light Brigades". To all intents and purposes, every municipality in the area of Banja Luka, that is, in the area of responsibility of the Banja Luka Corps, had not less than one Brigade, such Light Brigades, and in Banja Luka there were four Light Brigades in my time while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Prior to the reinforcement by the units of the 1st Krajina Corps, were the units that were conducting the Posavina corridor operation very effective in their combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The units that were at the beginning engaged in the operation of opening the corridor were not successful. A part of this was due to the small number of units committed; and a second reason, in my view, was that the units were concentrating more on plunder than on combat operations, and they also feared going into battle. If I can say so, that was the story going around us, among us officers in the command.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, there is a concern at this point about the considerable detail that you are going into, and perhaps you could explain what is the relevance. For example, if you are talking about events that occurred in 1991 and attempting to bring it forward, can you tell us -- once when I was talking to Mr. Tieger, I suggested that may be he tell us, give us a clue, as to what was at the end of the book and then we could understand, perhaps, the relevance. Of course, that is not the way we read books, but if you can give us a clue as to the relevance, just a short statement, it might help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Of course, the prior information was leading up to the command and control of the military forces within a particular region which is relevant to this case, and the requirements for reporting, the development of combat operations and how that was required to be proved and reported. As he was just testifying, those units that were then conducting these operations in the Posavina corridor in 1992 in the beginning were more concerned with plunder than they were with fighting. We are going then to develop whether or not the Corps had notice of that and whether it reported it to the main staff and what actions may or may not have been taken with regard to committing plunder, looting and some other issues that will come up further.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Suggesting responsibility, liability because of failure to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Showing actual notice, the ability to control.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What, on the part of Mr. Tadic? I mean, that is what we are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, not about Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It sounds more like a Royal Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It is going more to the issue, sir, of whether or not this was an international armed conflict and whether there was widespread and systematic attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think the testimony you elicited regarding the entry into Croatia on the way to Bihac is supportive of that point. Anyway, I encourage you to move as expeditiously -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Again which is why the testimony here that the units involved in Posavina, some of the units, came from the Republic of Croatia territory led by leaders from that area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That might be a convenient time to take the recess, your Honour, unless you want me to begin again?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We normally recess at 11.30. You are not the first person. It is 11.30. You may proceed. I do not want to cut you off, if that is where you are going. Thank you. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Did the Corps command receive reports that looting and the forced displacement of non-Serbs was going on in the area of operations in the Posavina corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the information on plunder of property and assets of non-Serb inhabitants and sometimes Serbs as well, I did see in the daily combat reports sent in by units from that region as well as units around Jajce; and the commanders or the command bodies reported about this at their regular briefings. We collected such information at the level of the Corps command in our daily reports and sent them to the command headquarters of the army of the Republika Srspka. In addition, the Assistant Commander in the Corps for morale and at lower levels regularly analysed reports about this, and this too was reported along the chain of command to the superior command. The security organs and other bodies of the Corps command received them, so that the main staff of the army of the Republika Srspka was informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the response to these reports by the Commander of the Corps and by the main staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The response was that such plunder and other negative tendencies should be halted or reduced to a minimum. However, we did not seem to succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did, in fact, the information that looting and forced displacement of non-Serbs was occurring in all three areas of operation continued throughout their duration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was reported regularly and it reached the main command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did either the Corps Commander or the main staff ever take any direct or effective action to prevent looting or forced displacement of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Formally and legally, measures were taken. The Commander of the main staff or, rather, the main staff of the army of the Republika Srpska gave orders to our Corps, and our Corps gave oral and written orders to subordinate units within the zone of responsibility of the 1st Corps. A military tribunal was formed with all its bodies. A large number of reports were collected, and many Commanders admitted criminal charges to responsible bodies, but I am not familiar whether any proceedings were started, whether they had any effect, whether measures were taken against individuals, but this was repeated endlessly. These lootings continued endlessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As a member of the Corps staff, were you ever notified that any military police or other authorities were sent to the field to arrest looters or those engaged in other criminal misconduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw such orders. In addition to looting, I must say that there was expulsions of people and cleansing of territory, and this was written in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever receive reports or hear or get notice that officials were sent out to the field and Commanders were arrested and placed in jail for allowing this conduct to be continued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not. I did not see such a report.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, may I ask a question regarding this because I may have lost some of the testimony. General Talic was a Commander of the 5th Corps Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was the Commander of the 5th Corps until it was renamed to the 1st Krajina Corps. Actually, it is the same Corps, only until May 1992 it was called the 5th Corps and after May, the 1st Krajina Corps of the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That included then the geographic area around Prijedor, did it, including Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If there were looting and an expulsion of persons from that area being committed by paramilitary groups, what responsibility would Commander Talic have with respect to those activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my view, when the 1st Corps or, rather, the 5th Corps was renamed into the 1st Corps, and from then General Talic was responsible for all operations in his zone of responsibility, area of responsibility, if he was familiar of the existence of paramilitary organisations and failed to do anything against them, in that way he actually legalized them and recognised them and included them in his own composition. Upon the -- when the 1st Krajina Corps was renamed, there were no longer paramilitary organisations as such. All this was known by the Corps, so it is no longer paramilitary, it is part of the regular force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What do you mean that there were no longer paramilitary groups in that area when the 5th Corps was renamed 1st Krajina Corps? Are you saying that they then became part of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They became part of the armoured forces in the area, and Talic could issue them orders and commit them and he did that and, if that was so, then it was no longer a paramilitary group; it was under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The TO became a part of the military, if I recall your testimony earlier, in May '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Territorial Defence units were simply ordered to drop that designation, TO, and from then on were called Light Brigades of the army of the Republika Srpska, that is 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you going to ask about the civilian police, Mr. Keegan? That is going beyond where you have been, but I had a question as to where they fit within this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Actually, ma'am, they were included within the earlier testimony about both TO and units, TO units and police.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Civilian police, did they became part of a military as well after May 1992 in terms of the responsibility of Colonel Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the civilian police was under the jurisdiction of the regular authorities in municipalities, but in case of need or their combat involvement, those units could be attached to or, rather, incorporated in Corps forces and engaged in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In such a case then the authority in the 1st Krajina, the top authority in the 1st Krajina, would be General Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Over the civilian police, should they have been engaging in the war activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only if they took part in combat, in combat operations. If they were performing their regular police tasks, then they were not under the Corps command.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Keegan. You may proceed. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): To clear that up then, Colonel Kranjc, if the police forces from Prijedor were included as part of the organisation or the force used in a military attack against a Local Commune such as Kozarac, in that situation they would fall under and be subject to the authority of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, under the responsibility of the Corps command or, rather, the highest level command in that region, and that was the 43rd Brigade or 343 Brigade in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You testified earlier that Brigade from the territory of Croatia, the area known as the Republic of Serb Krajina, took part in the battle in the Posavina corridor under the leadership of Martic. What time frame was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said this was about June 10th 1992 or a few days later. I said that from the territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina only one battalion came, not several units, just one battalion, which stayed for about 10 days. With that battalion was Martic and after that they returned via Banja Luka to Knin. There were no other units from that region, from the territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any artillery attacks conducted from the territory of the Serb Republic across the Drina River into Bosnia-Herzegovina after May 18th 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was talk about it in town, and on Radio Sarajevo that fire, artillery fire, was being opened from the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the territory of the Republic of Serbia towards the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In June and July 1992, did you begin to hear stories about events that had occurred in the Prijedor and Kozarac area earlier that summer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had already heard something about that at the beginning of June when I joined the Corps command, though that was a brief report, but there was more talk about it in town among the population at the end of June and July, about mass killings, looting and expulsions of Muslim population, especially from the region of Kozarac and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During that period did you have a conversation with Lieutenant Colonel Vaso Tepsic regarding the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was an official meeting of the Corps Commander with the closest associates which I also attended, and at which Colonel Tepsic Vaso, Assistant Corps Commander for Logistics, reported to the Commander that there were problems at the prisoners of war camp in Omarska regarding food and supply with drinking water for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During August 1992 did you see a large convoy of non-Serbs that were being taken out of the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was present when the convoy went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit 78, please, shown to the witness and placed on the elmo? (Exhibit 78 was handed to the witness) If it could be focused in closely in the central area? (To the witness): Colonel Kranjc, could you indicate on the map the area where you were when you saw this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was touring units of the 22nd Motorized Brigade which was capturing positions in the broader region of Vlasic. Upon returning from my tour on the road between Vlasic and Skender Vakuf, I noticed a long line consisting of passenger cars and buses headed by the police which gave us a sign to my driver and myself to move away and wait for the column to pass. That was near the village of Imljani which is on the map roughly here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So for the record that is below, Colonel, Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is south of Skender Vakuf, about seven or eight kilometres or five or six kilometres north of Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Vlasic, you referred to Vlasic Mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mount Vlasic, but we use that name for the whole region at the foot of the mountain and I can show you on the map what we refer to as "Vlasic". (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, the area which he was indicating basically encircles the "R" in the word "Herzegovina" on that map. What did you notice in this column -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, this is just on the map, it coincides with Herzegovina but it is still Bosnia. It is a part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was just referring to the location on this particular map. The word "Herzegovina" happens to be there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the letters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you notice about this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said already that at the head of the convoy was civilian police, not military police. On most vehicles the licence plates were of Prijedor opstina or municipality, and this can mean that the people, the passengers, need not necessarily have all been from Prijedor but from the region because the Prijedor licence plates covered several towns or opstinas around Prijedor. In the passenger cars (and there were several in the convoy) the passengers were sitting normally in their seats, more or less, and when the buses went past us the passengers in the buses lowered their heads. In my view, they probably had to do that because in each bus there was a policeman, and in the passenger cars there were no policemen and that is why they were not given orders to bow their heads. Most of the passengers in the buses were women, older people and children. In the passenger cars there were several men as well. Judging by the clothes, especially of the women, I could conclude that they were mostly Muslim women.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know where that convoy was headed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The convoy was moving in the direction of Vlasic. I will show you on the map. A point where Colonel, Lieutenant Colonel Pejovic, Commander of the 22nd Motorized Brigade, was carrying out exchange in various cases with Croatian forces that were located in the broader area of Travnik, that point is here. It is the junction. At that point, at that crossroads, an exchange was occasionally carried out of bodies, of casualties, between the Croat, Muslim and the Serb sides; and also here people were unloaded who were travelling in that direction and then they would go on foot on to Turbe and Travnik. Turbe is a little lower from the crossroads and Travnik is a little further on. As on that day Lieutenant Colonel Pejovic explained to me how this was being done and in what direction, when I saw this convoy I realised that it was travelling towards that juncture and that the people would get out of the buses and go in the direction of Turbe and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the approximate date that you saw this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was between the 10th and 15th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: A short time after this date, did you have a conversation with one of the other Deputy Commanders in the field about another convoy of non-Serbs being taken through that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that event when I saw this convoy, I decided not to work any longer in the army of the Republika Srspka, and not to go there any more. On August 18th, I ceased to work with the approval of the Corps Commander and a few days later Colonel Drago Rodic came to see me, Deputy Commander for the group of Light Brigades in Banja Luka -- he was a good friend of mine and a former associate -- and he told me that when he had travelled along that same road in the direction of Vlasic, his driver had said that he had heard that one such convoy, such as I had described, the policemen escorting the convoy had stopped it at a point which I will show you on the map -- it was just in front of a bend in the road -- and there was a precipice of about 150 to 200 metres deep, and that they had thrown in all the passengers into this, across this precipice, he did not know exactly, between 150 and 200 people; and Colonel Rodic said that he was ashamed of what had happened. That point was roughly here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Colonel, do not mark on the map, please. You may point to it but do not mark -- thank you -- unless the parties want you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. Let the record reflect that the witness is pointing to a point in the road approximately equal with the middle horizontal line in the letter "E" of "Herzegovina". (To the witness): Colonel Kranjc, did they indicate who the officials were involved with that convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was told by Colonel Rodic, this was the civilian police or militia, as we called it, from the Prijedor region. I do not know the exact location but from the Prijedor region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that would be a convenient time before we move into a new area?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I did not recall the date on that and I was looking at the monitor to see if I could pick it up. What was the date, Colonel, when you were told that this had occurred, well, not the date when were you told it had occurred, but on what date is it your understanding that it occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I saw the convoy that was between the 10th and 15th August, and at that time there was no talk about it and as I passed the vehicles I looked into the gorge and there was nothing to be seen, so in my opinion that event must have taken place between 15th and 20th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (11.30 a.m.) (Adjourned for a short time) (11.50 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you like to proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. ( To the witness): Colonel Kranjc, I would like to ask you a series of questions now regarding the public division of the JNA. Was there a difference in the way that the JNA and the federal authorities of the former Yugoslavia treated the withdrawal of the JNA in the various republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When the JNA withdrew from the Republic of Slovenia, did it intend to take all of its personnel and equipment with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And was it successful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In the Republic of Macedonia, similarly, did the JNA intend to take all of its personnel and equipment out of that when it withdrew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had the same intention there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In Croatia, did the JNA have a similar intent in the pull out from the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not have a similar intent there or, rather, it intended something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In areas where JNA had its units and garrisons until the proclamation of independence of the Republic of Croatia and where the Croats were the majority ethnic group, it intended and was preparing to withdraw all its equipment and troops; and in areas where the Serbs were the majority ethnic group, it intended to leave the major part of its troops and armaments and the explanation was that it was to serve the protection of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the JNA successful in this partial withdrawal from the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA successfully performed the task of leaving the major part of equipment and troops in areas where the Serbs were the majority group, that is, that was more or less successfully done, and in those parts where the Croats were the majority population, it did not succeed in carrying out its task, its intentions, in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened in those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time the Republic of Croatia already had its army, its armoured forces, and they surrounded most of the garrisons and barracks and part of units managed to get out of these garrisons, these barracks, by fighting, by force, and other units negotiated the pull-out of the units and equipment, and some units and parts of command surrendered to the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina what was the JNA intent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA's intent was similar to the one in the Republic of Croatia. In other words, in those areas where the Serbs were not a majority, it wanted to pull out from those areas the major part of its troops and equipment; and those areas where Serbs were the majority and where the Republika Srpska was already formed or was in the making, they wanted to leave behind the major part of the troops and equipment. This is largely what happened, that is what was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In fact, could you say that with regard to the area of the territory of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that the JNA left, in effect, complete armies within those regions where they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The term "army" is not an adequate term, but it left behind Corps and lower rank, lower echelon, units. If I may explain it, what is a Corps and what is an army? A unit, such as Banja Luka Corps, is a unit subordinate to the command of the Military District or the army command. In Sarajevo, there was the Military District command; whereas in Bosnia there were three Corps, Sarajevo, Tuzla and Banja Luka Corps, and the JNA managed to pull out the major part of troops and equipment from the area of the Tuzla and Sarajevo, of course, whereas the major part of the troops and weaponry of the 5th Corps, that is, then the 1st Krajina Corps remain there. So it did pull out part of the Corps and equipment and armaments and part of it remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Regarding the public announcement of a division of the JNA and the pull out of Yugoslav forces from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you ever see an order directing all members of the JNA who were not from Bosnia-Herzegovina to leave the territory of that Republic by 19th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw only the order affecting the members of the unit, that is, the Educational Centre for armoured and mechanized unit and units under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the order to transfer the school back to the territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, first, there was the order in the course of April that the Educational Centre was to stand prepared with all the strength and facilities and equipment for the transfer to the Republic of Serbia, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then it was followed by an order which came in May which somewhat modified the previous order, in the sense that men were to go and as for the equipment only what could be transferred to a far Yugoslavia by air, because land routes towards far Yugoslavia were already closed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How many members of the staff of the school actually left and went to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On May 19th, that was the day when the troops were to leave and part of the equipment was to go to Yugoslavia, between 25 to 30 officers left for Yugoslavia and a certain number of civilians serving in JNA, they left for Belgrade. Later on, those who stayed behind for a while in the area of the 5th Corps also left for Yugoslavia and joined the army of Yugoslavia on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You yourself were transferred to the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 12th or 13th May, I was ordered by the head of the Personnel Administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, General Krstic, the head of the Administration had signed it on 11th May, and I was ordered by this order to surrender my duty to the Commander of the armoured and mechanized units and to assume, to take over the same post that I occupied before in the operational body of the staff of the 5th Corps. At that time it was still called officially the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That post with the Operational section of the 5th Corps, you were just a member of that section, not the head of a section, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was Assistant Head of the Operational Educational Department in the staff of -- the Assistant Head of that department for Operational Educational affairs in the headquarters of 5th Corps. That was my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With respect to the operational units of the JNA in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, in particular, in the 5th Corps, rather than ordering the general withdrawal of all officers of the Yugoslav forces, were the officers instead encouraged to stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not see or hear of an order for their relocation or the sending of the troops, that generally that all of them should be included in the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there after 19th May 1992 any significant change or any change at all in the staff of the 5th Corps which later became the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took up this duty on 2nd June in the command of what was already renamed into the 1st Krajina Corps, and I found there all the officers and all the other troops who were there a year ago, a year earlier, while I was still in the command who were there, I again found them in the Corps, and the same held true of the Commanders of Battalions, Brigades and other officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there a difference between how officers and soldiers or conscripts were treated under this public division of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, soldiers who at that time, that is, in May '92, for instance, were serving their military service in the area of the Republika Srpska or, rather, in the area of the 5th Corps and were not native to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were enabled and provided with a possibility of return to their republics, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was this a fear that the conscripted soldiers might not be willing to fight as aggressively for a republic that was not their home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a fear, but there were also regulations that a person who was not a national of a state could not serve in the army of that other state, because Serbs had proclaimed the Republika Srpska as their state and those soldiers who were nationals of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were not nationals of the Republika Srpska. So that both by virtue of the military regulations both before and during the war, that was prescribed it in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you ever officially assigned to an entity known as the Republika Srpska or its army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, I already said that, ordered by the head of the Personnel Administration of the Federal Secretariat, transferred from the Educational Centre, which was the only such centre of the JNA, to the 5th Corps command which at that time also was a part of the JNA. In this manner I was merely transferred from one JNA unit to another JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At any time did you ever have to take a new loyalty oath to army of the Republika Srpska or the Republika Srpska itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody ever asked me to take a new oath of allegiance or to repeat an oath of allegiance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did any officer that you knew of ever have to take any such loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that anyone was invited to take a new oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What uniform did you wear while you were on duty after 19th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I and my friends continued to wear the same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is the army of the JNA, the uniform of the army -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army, except that since the main staff of the ARS had ordered that the insignia of that army had to be put on, most of the officers did put on these insignia, they were mostly on their caps and on the arm, did that, but I did not and I did not have any problems because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did others also continue to wear the insignia of the JNA on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some of the officers did continue to wear the former insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there ever any problems created by that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody had any problems because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As far as it was understood by the officers in the 1st Corps and other units that you were associated with, what was the socio-political goal of the armed conflict that the various groups of the former Yugoslav Army engaged in in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, deriving from conversations with people and my fellow officers, the goal was to join, to unite, with the Republic of Yugoslavia territorially at first and then to become the joint armoured forces of Yugoslavia sooner or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So the goal to rejoin these three parts of the JNA was the goal of the officers and the staff members of the army that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only the commands, but people talked about it, troops talked about it, that they considered themselves a part of Yugoslavia and that they wanted to join it, first, to secede, to separate, from the already recognised Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then join Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So is it fair to say then that the goal or the role that the officers of the 1st Corps and others that you knew saw themselves in was that they continued and remained to be a part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now some questions about the following situation. Consider that there is a man of Serb dissent of military age, that is, between the ages of 25 to 45, let us say, who lives in an opstina in the Banja Luka region in the period of May to June 1992, do you believe it is possible that the SDS leadership in the Banja Luka region would permit such a person who had fled from his Local Commune just before the start of combat operations in that commune because he did not want to fight against the non-Serbs in that territory -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I raise one matter before the witness answers the question and that really -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Wait. I do not think the question has been completed. Finish the question and before I allow the witness to answer, I will hear your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In that situation, would it be possible that that person could return to that Local Commune approximately three/four weeks later, after the completion of combat operations, to become the President of the SDS in that Local Commune, Secretary of the Local Commune and a member of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Colonel. Do you have an objection, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, your Honour. It is a very long question that has been asked to this witness involving a number of different issues. As I see it, there has been no foundation or ground work as to why this witness should particularly give his opinion on this matter. He is being asked to comment on the position within the SDS of a hypothetical male within a certain range of ages who may have committed particular acts, such as fleeing from his area, without any basis being given as to why he should give that opinion in relation to this particular matter. We have heard no detailed evidence as to the knowledge of this witness relating to the SDS and what he can tell us about it to qualify him to give that opinion. It seems to me an opportunity for the Prosecution to make such a statement in relation to a hypothetical situation that we all know what he is getting at and to have some sort of comment by the witness without any proper foundation for that opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If it please the court -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is a long objection, but what I would like you to focus on is this witness' knowledge about the SDS hierarchy and the way that it operates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will go further into foundational questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He has certainly talked a lot about the JNA, but let us look at SDS. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Colonel Kranjc, in addition to your service in the Banja Luka region, were you a candidate for the Municipal Assembly in Banja Luka in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the first so-called democratic elections in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990, the Party for Democratic Changes in Banja Luka nominated me and included me in their list of nominees for the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, even though I was not a member of that Party. The Party won a sufficient number of votes so that I was the seventh nominee on the list, it won 17 seats in the Municipal Assembly, so I was a council man, I was a member of the Municipal Assembly for more than a year until I resigned this duty in the Municipal Assembly. So, for more than a year I was in touch with the operation of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka and the activities of all parties. As shortly afterwards I had become the Commander of the head of the Educational Centre, owing to my personal contacts, or official contacts, I met the majority of the leaders or the members and leaders of the SDS in Banja Luka as well as the mode of operation of that Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 141 could be shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: While that is being shown to the witness, the translation indicated that he was with the Party for Democratic Changes; that is the SDS, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, that is not correct, your Honour. I will explain that when we see Exhibit 141. (Exhibit 141 was handed to the witness) (To the witness): Colonel Kranjc, if you could review that exhibit? What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the issue of the official gazette of the municipality of Banja Luka, 9th November 1990, No. 9, page 192; the announcement on the joint list. Do you want me to read it through or?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could simply place it on the elmo, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a list which the parties submitted as the list of its nominees for the members of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka municipality. As I have said, my name is the seventh on the list. In addition to the Reformist Party, our Party was the only Party which was not a monoethnic Party. As you can see, there were Croats, Serbs, Yugoslavs, Slovenes, Muslims and so on and so forth; and SDS, SDA and HDZ were monoethnic parties. The lists of their nominees were monoethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Kranjc. If you could place the English translation, please, on that section of the screen? The first section was titled "The list of candidates of the League of Communists of Bosnia-Herzegovina Socialist Democratic Party and Democratic Socialist Alliance of Bosnia-Herzegovina". That was the Party that you were nominated from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. During the year that you spent in the Assembly, I believe you have already stated you had contact with the leadership of the SDS and the other parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you familiar with their positions and their platform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The platform of each Party was publicly -- made public before the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was it also clear from your contacts with members of the SDS as to who they would consider to be appropriate members of the Party, what the requirements would be for a Serb to be a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this happened at meetings that I attended. This also happened and there was talk about it at meetings of the Municipal Assembly and also on other occasions, and in the newspaper it was stated what they wanted, what their Party was struggling for, the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there, in fact, a public provocation or threat, if you will, published in the newspapers against you and other members of the 1st Corps by members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The leader of the Banja Luka SDS Vukic mentioned me as well as a number of other members of the Banja Luka Corps, attacking me in the papers, the Banja Luka Glas, when he through the journalist called on Kranjc, Hasotic, Osman Selak and Radman Zvonko must leave the army, at that time it was still the JNA, and that he would see to it in the Corps command that people like that would no longer remain in the Banja Luka Corps. This was repeated several times only in different words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When they referred to "people like that" was that the fact that you were not a Serb and therefore could not be considered loyal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they otherwise knew me as a Commander, but that Vukic in person, his interests were not served for a Slovene to be a Commander of the Educational Centre, even though at that time the JNA still officially existed, because those attacks in the media, in the press and radio were mostly in February, March, April. In May there were not any as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was it clear from your comments and your contact with the leaders of the SDS whether they would allow someone to be part of the leadership of the SDS who was, whose goal was peaceful coexistence with non-Serbs in the region of Bosanski Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Publicly they did not say that, but in more intimate circles that was their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: More particularly, when the armed conflict began starting in the territory of the Republic of Croatia and moving into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it become more apparent that any Serb who refused to participate in that activity would not be considered a loyal member and, therefore, entitled to representation in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
