utterances.text: Certainly he could not become, because SDS and all the power and all the bodies and the people believed the same, that their army was one and that it had to be respected and obeyed and everything had to be done in favour of it and one should participate in it, whoever was called up should go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Back to the hypothetical which I had posed to you earlier is ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you are going to repeat the same question, I think we have a record of it, let me hear from Mr. Kay as to whether he still has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Much obliged, your Honour. The position is that this witness had been a member of the municipal party for one year, having stood in the elections for a different party of a party of the SDS to which the question is directed, and the issue of the status of the Kozarac SDS may be an entirely different position from that of the SDS leadership which is what the questions from my learned friend have been directed at whilst laying this foundation. There may be worlds apart in relation to the SDS leadership and the position of the SDS in a small area such as Kozarac where we know that some 141 members took part in the plebiscite in November 1991. What I am concerned with here is that witnesses are going to have hypothetical questions put to them in such a way that matters of fact to be determined by this Tribunal to a certain extent are going to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will overrule your objection, Mr. Kay. You are correct that we are talking about Kozarac, what happened in Kozarac. As I recall the testimony, however, there was significant control, if not absolute control, from the regional office in Banja Luka where this witness is from, notwithstanding, as I recall, a Statute that prohibited such direction and that came from at least one other witness. That is my memory of the testimony. So that even though there was an SDS in Kozarac, this gentleman is in Banja Luka. My recollection of the testimony is that there was significant control and direction from the regional headquarters, even though it was prohibited by Statute. The other matter, if I may just say, most importantly -- well, Mr. Keegan, you correct me if I am wrong first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I am not going to correct your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Particularly if I am going to overrule the direction, but did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The hypothetical of course, first of all, did not relate directly to Kozarac; it related to the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But the hypothetical person is leaving Kozarac and coming back, is he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, I did not mention the specific village. I said a Local Commune in the Banja Luka region. The second issue is of course the testimony of the witness ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me cut you off. If it does not relate then to the Kozarac Local Commune, what is the relevance of it, back to Judge Stephen's concern earlier this morning about expanding questions and testimony beyond what we are immediately concerned with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In point of fact, your Honour, the following questions were going to relate to the fact that the Banja Luka SDS regional authorities controlled the SDS positions for the region. I simply had not gotten that far through the testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But we have heard it from other testimony, at least I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct, which is why I was going to cut it off and not disagree with what you said. In addition, of course, as I understand, you have overruled the objection, so I will just continue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Our rules of evidence, Rule 89 particularly, allow, as we have indicated before, the admission of relevant testimony that is probative. We will overrule the objection, admit the response and give it the appropriate weight that we consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour will appreciate that I am concerned with relevance as your Honour has mentioned in the ruling just now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I did not hear you object on the grounds of relevance. What I hear though, and I am particularly concerned about what happened in Kozarac, however, Kozarac is within the region of Banja Luka, so it has overall relevance. I certainly wish we would get a little closer to Kozarac though. I overrule your objection on that basis as well. Mr. Keegan, do you want the question read back or can you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Colonel Kranjc, to continue with the hypothetical which I presented to you earlier, the situation of a Serb man of military age who lives in an opstina in the Banja Luka region in the period of May to June 1992, is it possible that such a person could flee from his local commune just before the start of combat operations there and return approximately three weeks later, and at that point be appointed to the position of the President of the SDS in that Local Commune, the Secretary of the Local Commune and a member of the Reserve Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion that was not possible. Your Honours, if I may be permitted I would make a remark. Kozarac as a Local Commune belongs to the opstina of Prijedor and not the opstina of Banja Luka. There may be some lack of clarity because occasionally there is talk of the Banja Luka region which in certain respects included the Prijedor region, but sometimes we talk of the Prijedor region which covered from Bosanski Novi towards Dubica, Sanski Most and Klucj, about halfway between Banja Luka and Prijedor. It is true that Kozarac as a local commune did not belong to Banja Luka but to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Prijedor opstina or the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Prijedor, the opstina of Prijedor included the Local Commune of Kozarac, and occasionally the expression the "Prijedor region" is used which is broader than the opstina but which leans on the city of Prijedor in the economic, health, educational and in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is the Prijedor opstina in the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because Banja Luka called itself the seat of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and Prijedor was part of that region, but sometimes it was just called the Banja Luka region and sometimes it was called the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina. It depended on the way in which the people used the term. Officially it was the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina which included all the opstinas in which the majority were Serbs, or rather in which the assemblies, the majority was held by the SDS, so that that municipality could vote in favour of joining the Autonomous Region. This did not happen in Prijedor because at the elections in 1990 the party of Democratic Action or the so-called SDA party won in which the majority or all were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan in your question when you asked whether this was within the Banja Luka region, did you mean that to constitute the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina? Were you using the Banja Luka region that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I was using the Banja Luka region in that way, your Honour, to separate the transformation when the Autonomous Region of Bosanski Krajina later became part of the Republika Srpska. Rather than get into that confusion, I was simply trying to contain it to the Banja Luka area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. I just wanted to know when you said "Banja Luka region" did you mean the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina and the answer is yes, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, as that is understood, that term.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And as the witness understands it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One further question just to clarify your question, you are confining it to some hypothetical person who flees, with all that that word connotes, and flees for a particular reason which you have stated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct. Recalling earlier your testimony, Colonel Kranjc, which party controlled the government of the autonomous region of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was fully controlled only by the SDS party, the Serbian Democratic Party which was headquartered in Banja Luka headed by Brdjanin and Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If at some point the Serbian members of the opstina Prijedor Assembly formed their own Serbian Assembly of the opstina Prijedor and voted to join the Autonomous Region of the Krajina, in your opinion then would they necessarily fall under the authority of the SDS leaders in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Again considering all of those factors, would your answer still be the same if in this Banja Luka region, that is the Autonomous Region of the Krajina, this individual fled the opstina to avoid the combat actions in that opstina returned three to four weeks later after the completion of those operations, would the SDS allow that person to become the President of the SDS in that commune, Secretary of that Local Commune and a member of the Reserve Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could not become that except if upon instructions or assignments from the SDS he went somewhere else on an important assignment for the needs of the SDS, but normally he could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now if that person had in fact participated in such combat operations in the opstina where he was from and where he later became the President of the SDS, would that participation necessarily be noted in his official military service book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. Perhaps it was not possible because of the shortage of time, the slowness of the administrative bodies and because most things were being done or resolved by oral agreements and orders and less through paperwork.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In your opinion then during this time frame when the armed conflicts were occurring in 1992 in that region, could someone point to his military book indicating no notation of an assignment to a specific unit involved in combat operations and use that as proof that he was not involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I am sorry, the question was could the lack of a notation be used as proof that he was not involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He has already answered the question and that certainly is a legal question as to whether it can be used as proof, but I think he answered earlier that it did not necessarily mean that, that because of what was going on at that time the decisions were made orally. So I will object for you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am much obliged.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can rephrase it if you insist on asking the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour. During this time frame May/June of 1992, was it possible that just anyone could join the Reserve Police in the local area instead of going to a regular combat unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not quite understand the question. Could it be repeated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. During this time frame May/June 1992, was it possible that just any individual could simply show up and join the Reserve Police as an excuse from regular combat duty or assignments or an exception from those assignments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible if he had certain connections or certain reasons for rewarding him he could avoid his military obligation in a real combat unit and remain in a police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were these positions in the Reserve Police checked and controlled to ensure the nature or quality of people who were permitted to join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was control for the civilian police but also those who were sent to the military police as the municipal or local police were under the direct influence or rather competence of the ruling party and the administrative bodies, then they checked especially to make sure who was entering those most narrow circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was it possible that factors such as political connections or money could enable someone to gain those jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was it possible during the time frame of May/June 1992 for a Serb to leave his opstina in the Banja Luka region, the Autonomous Region of the Krajina and go to Banja Luka itself to be issued a weapon and ammunition by the Banja Luka Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible too, because some received weapons from several sources; not just one weapon but several.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would it be more likely if the person was a trusted or influential member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, what do you mean? A higher rank member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A member of a higher rank? You are thinking of somebody who has a higher position in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, a higher position or greater influence in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was normal. It is probably normal in some other organisations that the person who has a higher position has greater privileges, greater possibilities to get an easier job, an easier assignment, one less exposed to the danger of war and yet hold a responsible position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Defence exhibit 8, please. (Defence Exhibit 8 was handed the witness). Colonel Kranjc, if you could turn to page 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you explain what the section, the noted Section 13 is for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Section 13 represents data on the secession of military obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now if someone received a work obligation assignment giving him civilian responsibilities in lieu of a specific military assignment, would that have to be noted in this portion of the military book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was someone with a work assignment in lieu of military responsibility still considered to be conducting or completing his military responsibility for service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So in that instance would the section regarding the termination of military service be filled in before they finished that work obligation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle yes, but at that time some administrative matters were not resolved quickly. People were transferred from one post to another without the whole procedure, that was obligatory reporting to one unit from another, being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If this section was then filled in and completed, would it not mean that the person had completed their work assignment in lieu of military duties and therefore had completed their military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if this booklet were to be filled in then it would mean what you say, but the termination of a military obligation may cease on several grounds, health, other things, permanent inability or old age, and then it has to be noted on the basis of which article the military obligation ceases. The responsible body must enter here, in these two places, reference to the article of the law on military obligation certification on deletion from the records is being done, and a date has to be added and the stamp and signature of the authorised person. Then it is a complete procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Let the record reflect that the witness pointed to the first two blank lines for the location where the articles of the law of military service would have to be filled in, and then the obvious state line for the date and signature. Thank you, Colonel Kranjc. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we just stay on this matter please, Colonel. Looking at Section 13 of the military book, that would be completed, would it not, when someone was discharged from military obligation for all time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For all times or temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All time. You are discharged from your military service for a particular reason under the military code?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said he can be discharged for all times or for a certain time, and that can be told from the number of the article of the law on the military obligation. I do not know exactly all the articles of that law, but the person certifying such a case, and I am referring to the person signing this, he has before him the law, he studies the law and finds the article on the grounds of which a person will be discharged. I cannot say all the articles that are applied in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it could be applied or completed for a temporary discharge from military service as well as a final discharge from military service; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If someone is excused military service and this is not completed, what would be the problem for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that person is really subject to one of the laws, one of the articles of the law on military service and which envisages excuse from military service and if he proves this with the necessary documents, then he would have no problems, but if someone did not have the necessary documents or if those documents were inaccurate or if he managed to achieve that excuse through good connections ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- and he received this signature, then sooner or later this would be discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if it came to it that you were required to show that you were excused from military service and you wanted to be excused from military service, you could provide the documentation and have this completed if you were called upon to perform that service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, that would be a convenient moment. I do not think I have any further questions, but I would like to review the matter, if possible, over the luncheon adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. You will be given that opportunity. We will stand in recess until 2.30. (1.00) (Luncheon Adjournment) PRIVATE (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff is sitting. I wanted to say we missed you this morning. Mr. Kay, would you like to continue with the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have completed my cross-examination. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Nothing in redirect, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Colonel, there is one question you can perhaps help me on: at the time that the order was given for the members of the JNA who were not Bosnians to return to Yugoslavia, to the rump Yugoslavia, there was also an order given for those who were Bosnians to remain in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I gather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Microphone, please). Your Lordships, I only saw the order about the relocation of the personnel and equipment of the Educational Centre, since it was the Educational Centre for armoured and mechanized units of the JNA at large. The order specified and made it possible for the troops born or from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina could go to Yugoslavia, not only those from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, but even those whose home was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they could go to Yugoslavia, but that applied to the Educational Centre and the Commanders and the officers working at the Educational Centre. I was also offered the choice of going to Yugoslavia or remaining in that position.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I see. Of course, when you say they could remain in Bosnia or they could go to Yugoslavia, that would mean that they would go to particular specified units, I suppose, would they? They would not just become civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it meant that the superiors in the Educational Centre who would be leaving Banja Luka to Yugoslavia, they were all told they would continue in the same posts in the Educational Centre at a new location.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Those that chose to remain in Bosnia, were they allocated to particular units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those officers from the Educational Centre who did not want to go to Yugoslavia were also ordered, but then on an individual basis from the Personnel Administration in Belgrade for their temporary allocation to new posts in the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not catch the last words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: 5th Corps, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Colonel, when the Red Berets became part of the VRS, did they take their orders from the VRS Corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, there was the command of the then 1st Krajina Corps. I would not know exactly whom they received the orders from. In case of orders for combat operations, then it was from the Corps command. If it applied to some other activities, then it would be from the political authorities or the local authorities in the region of Banja Luka. Barracks which belonged to my command, that is, the Educational Centre were twice surrounded. They were the facilities in the centre of the town, and the barracks of Krajina Brigades which was some seven kilometres to the north of Banja Luka; and because stories began to spread that the JNA was about to pull out the equipment and materiel from these barracks to Belgrade, so that somebody in the town launched this action and the next day the Red Berets blocked the barracks, both barracks. I intervened immediately with the Crisis Staff and, after a brief conversation, these blocks were removed. In some other instances, somebody else, that is, somebody also issued orders to the Red Berets except the Corps command.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were these Red Berets Serbs from Serbia or were they Bosnian Serbs or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that exactly and, therefore, I cannot give you an accurate answer. Personally, I think they were from the area of Banja Luka and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Colonel, there is one other question arising out of your evidence. I think you said that one reason why in May '92 soldiers of the 5th Corps were ordered to return to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and one reason was that by law they were not able to serve in what was a foreign state, namely, Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is so, and I quoted it as the second reason because, formally or legally speaking, there were two states proclaimed, the Republika Srpska and Yugoslavia on the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I think, if I am right, that you said that applied to soldiers. What about officers because, clearly, officers did serve with Republika Srpska which was a foreign state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the legal point of view, this would also hold true of the officers, evidently, but under the previous orders they were only temporarily assigned and, as far as I know, nobody ever raised that question either from the legal point of view or from any other. If somebody opted for staying there, he was allowed to do so. It was made possible for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have one question and that has to do with the Yugoslav People's Army. After Croatia and Slovenia and Bosnia-Herzegovina gained their independence, I gather that all that was left of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, was based in the Federal Socialist Republic of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer this question legally or formally speaking. Until May 19th there was one JNA or, at least as far as we are concerned as regards the documents that I had all received, there was also JNA in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that it was divided into two, both in two states, that is, two armies. As I had received orders some 10 days before that where to report, and that it even specified that I was to report to the 5th Corps, that is the old name because the army of the Republic of Srpska had not been proclaimed again. I accepted that. But, apart from that, every officer, apart from this official part of the official order, there was also something else that we were supposed to do that, that is, some superior reasons for which we should either stay there or move elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? What "superior reasons that we should either stay there or move elsewhere"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not say -- I meant other reasons, family reasons and the like.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who was the supreme Commander of the Yugoslav People's Army then in Serbia after May 22nd 1992? In the United States, for example, the President of the United States is the Commander-in-Chief of the military forces. Who was the supreme Commander of the Yugoslav People's Army on May 22nd 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen the constitution of that new Yugoslavia after May 92 but, as far as one can learn from the media, television, papers, the Commander-in-Chief, formally or legally, was the President of the Republic of Yugoslavia. At first it was Dobrica Cosic, and then a new President came because the former presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia composed first of eight members and then, after the independence of the four Republics, was abolished.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, ma'am, nothing further

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the Colonel being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Then Colonel Kranjc, you may be permanently excused. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Lordships, thank you very much for inviting me to give my testimony here. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to mention something at this stage. I will not be taking the next witness, but there is a matter that I wanted to mention. We are now today, this afternoon, filing a motion in relation to a particular witness that we expect to testify next week, seeking orders for protective measures. I just announce it now; your Honours will receive it this afternoon, I should imagine. I announce it now because it is at such short notice. The witness is coming next week and the motion will mention the reason why it has come up so soon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will locate the motion then. I am glad you have told us that you filed it. That means we will then assure that we get it this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Jerko Doko, your Honour. MR. JERKO DOKO, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Doko, would you please take the oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I speak? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Doko you maybe seated. Mr. Keegan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Doko, would you please state for the record your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jerko Doko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 14th September 1952.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you born in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the former territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Are you currently a resident of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you grow up in the area around Mostar in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and attend the University of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I lived in Mostar until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you complete your compulsory military service in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Between 1976 and 1990 did you serve in the reserves and in the Mostar TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the staff of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Mostar. I was the head of the Department for Nuclear, Biological and Chemical Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you have the rank of Captain 1st Class?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you also serve as the Chef de Cabinet for the first elected Mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Subsequent to that were you appointed as the Minister of Defence for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 1st February 1991 I took up the post of the Minister of Defence of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Until when did you serve in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 13th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you arrived to your post on 1st February 1991, what were the main duties of the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main duties of the Minister of Defence were at the time to reorganise the Ministry of Defence and keep the control of the Ministry of Defence, the mobilization, the forces in our Republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At the time that you took your office was there a conflict between the Republic and the Federal authorities regarding who had control over the mobilization of Republic forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was shortly before the elections in November 1990. The Federal Assembly changed the law on National Defence specifying that the laws on mobilization and records should be taken over by the army authorities which the Republican government and Assembly did not go along with after the elections. So that was the conflict of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the composition and the purpose of the TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina under the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was one of the components of the armed forces of the former SFRY. It had Republican headquarters which were responsible politically and operationally to the then Executive Councils and presidencies of the then Republics, and for military, in military matters, they were responsible to the JNA General Staff. We had eight districts. Our Territorial Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina was divided into eight districts. It had its Republic headquarters, and zonal and municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the purpose that the TO was supposed to serve under the old system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As its name says, the Territorial Defence was to protect the territory. The troops in the territory were expected to protect that territory. All financial and material support was provided by Republican governments, that is, Executive Councils to these units of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that why the original law had the control for mobilization of that TO within the Republic authority and not the Federal authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The jurisdiction of the mobilization should be in the hands of the civilian authorities rather than army authorities because the Republican agencies and the government were to take care of this, of the economic and working ability on individual parts of the territory, and it was quite logical for them to do that rather than Belgrade or the army, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you arrived at your post who was acting as the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before me, the Minister of Defence was General Fetagic, a JNA General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the majority of his staff also JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were; his Chef de Cabinet was a civilian and Assistant for Civilian Affairs was a civilian. All the other assistants and associates were JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At the time you took your office, who had control of the weapons of the Republic TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As early as the beginning of 1990 the orders arrived, that the weapons be taken over by the JNA and placed in its depots for the sake of better storage or better keeping. To my mind, it meant the disarmament of the Territorial Defence. It was done in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia by the committee of the then parties, and governments of Slovenia did not allow it and they did have their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What effect did the ability of Slovenia of its TO to arm itself have when Slovenia declared independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Yugoslav People's Army attacked Slovenia, their Minister, Janez Jansa, mobilized the Territorial Defence, dressed them up and armed them, and that is why it took them only four days to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you arrived at your post who was in command of the Republic TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commander was a Serb, General -- I cannot remember his name now. He was there for a short time only. He was there only for a month and then they brought another, General Drago Vukosavljevic, a JNA General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The original General who was in position at the command of the TO when you took office, was he sympathetic to the Republic position regarding mobilization or the Federal position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He supported the Republic position and held a working meeting with me where the Ministry of Defence and the Defence Staff had to discuss the plans for the training of units for the materiel, supply of equipment and things like that, and I think that was why they replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: General Vukosavljevic, was he sympathetic to the Republican position or to the Federal position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was sympathetic of the Federal position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina approve the appointment of General Vukosavljevic to the position of the Commander of the TO of the Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the multi-Party elections, since national parties HDZ, SDA and SDS won a majority in the Assembly, they divided up the key posts amongst themselves so that the Defence Ministry was given to a representative of the Croat people, of the Internal Affairs to a representative of the Muslim people and the Staff Commander was to be a representative of the Serb people and the JNA General Staff proposed that the Drago Vukosavljevic or, rather, appointed him, and the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As a senior government official in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you follow all of the sessions of the Assembly of the Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was my duty as a member of the government to follow work in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In the second half of 1991 and continuing through the first part of 1992, did the political differences in the Assembly become divisive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the basic causes for this division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the major causes at the time was whether this particular law on mobilization and recruitment, whether we should apply the Federal law or, as most of us wanted, that it should be the internal affair of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that we should have control over the recruitment of our boys and the mobilization of our people. That was one of the major problems causing differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the issue of the independence of the Republic itself also one of the major issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it figured in the Assembly debates. It was the main, the ultimate goal of all of us to have the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was opposed by members of the SDS Party, because they wanted something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was a final vote reached on whether the Republic would accept the Federal law on mobilization or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this occurred on 29th February and 1st March 1992. A referendum was carried out in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this was later confirmed in the Assembly when, by a majority of votes, the independence was voted for. The members of the SDS walked out of the Assembly upon the call of their President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What occurred in the streets of Sarajevo after the walk out by the members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Barricades began to be put up by members or organised by members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What steps were then taken to form the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We undertook to elaborate a law on National Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was later adopted at the Assembly, in which it was stated that the armed forces would be comprised of Territorial Defence, the already existing defence forces in the south, HVO, we had HOS units, and all those groups which would defend Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as the armed forces of the Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: By that do you mean police forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During this same time, shortly after the walk out of the Assembly and the initiation of the law to form the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did the JNA begin taking up positions around the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA, among other things, focused on a blockade of Sarajevo, a siege of Sarajevo. It did so even before; it prepared structures for artillery weapons on the surrounding hills around Sarajevo. When we insisted they give us an explanation, they said it was for the purpose of an exercise of the army for the protection of the city and we know what happened later, they shelled the city, and afterwards they handed over those weapons to Karadzic's SDS forces which destroyed Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Doko, I notice that you have pulled out some notes on the table from your briefcase. Did you prepare some aide memoirs to assist you with the facts, figures, the numbers, dates and locations of information you are going to testify to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As my testimony contains a large number of data, I would not like to misinterpret them, so I put them on paper so, if necessary, I can convey them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this document shown to the witness, please, and mark the next Exhibit 180? (Exhibit 180 was handed to the witness) (To the witness): Mr. Doko, do you recognise Exhibit 180, that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that the aide memoir that you prepared yourself to assist you in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With an English translation attached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender Exhibit 180.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seems to me it is not technically an exhibit. It is an aide memoir of the witness which has an entirely different status. It is not material arriving from the background of the case, but something to help him with his testimony in court. The court may feel that there is a distinction as to the need for it to be an exhibit and to assist him in giving his account.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There is no problem, as far as I am concerned, with him using notes, if he needs them, to assist him in responding to questions, as long as you have a copy of it and you are entitled to that. As to whether it need be admitted, typically, it would not -- of course, we do not have any rules on this, but ......

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. Normally, I would not offer it, but given this system I assumed you might want it as part of the record and, therefore, I offered it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have an objection, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not think there is a need for it to be part of the record as it may be something that can become overused. I can foresee that there would be no limit if we were to embark on this line at this stage, because the aide memoir of a witness rather than his exhibits to be produced relating to the actual case itself is a distinction.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, in my system it would not be admissible. Let me confer with my fellow judges since there is no rule on the point and let us see if we can get a consensus. (The learned Judges conferred) I sustain your objection, Mr. Kay. It appears that our systems are more alike than they are unlike and, as I have indicated, there is no rule on the point. We want to hear from the witness and so it is important. It is like a prior deposition maybe in your system that he may have given. That would not come in if he is here to testify. You may, of course, if there was a statement that he gave before, and I am sure it was, and it was not what has been marked for identification as 180, you may use that for impeachment purposes or, if you wish, you may take a look at that statement if he is using it to refresh his recollection. But we do not want it as an exhibit, so I will sustain the objection. That is one piece of paper we will not have to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Fine, your Honour, thank you. (To the witness): After the passage of the law on defence in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, how did your Ministry go about forming the staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and who held those positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 6th April 1992, we took over the offices of the former headquarters of Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we undertook to form a new staff which would be loyal to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that would organise the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The head of the staff was at the time -- I must have a look, I forget names -- Hasan Efendic, he was formally in the municipal city of Sarajevo, he was the Commander of the staff, by nationality a Muslim; Stjepan Siber, a Colonel who used to work in the former TO staff, he expressed loyalty to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was one of the deputies; another equal deputy was Colonel Jovan Divjak, by nationality a Serb. Therefore, the Commander was a Muslim, the deputies, a Croat and Serb, and the structure of the staff was 25 Croats, 10 to 11 Serbs and the rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At this point which you had created a staff and declared the existence of the armed forces, had the Republic been able to gain control of its weapons back from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we could not get the weapons. They did not want to have any contact with us; and the former staff in collaboration with the army Corps in the field issued weapons to the municipal TO staff with a majority Serb population and mobilized those units in those opstinas which we were not informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In July 1992, did the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina officially become the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO and police forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question? I did not quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In July 1992, did the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina officially become known as the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO and separate police forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would like to go back to some questions regarding the start of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. In September 1991 was there a vote of the presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia regarding a declaration of martial law for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was a rump presidency of SFRY where the representative of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia were not present. Only four remained, representatives of Serbia, Montenegro, Kosovo and Macedonia. It was known as the "rump" presidency and it passed decisions on the commitment of JNA units and the re-deployment of the forces from Slovenia and Croatia in the direction of Bosnia-Herzegovina and further, which was unacceptable for us because that presidency did not represent the whole of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was one person clearly identified as being the leader of those four members of the presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that rump presidency was headed by the representative of Montenegro, Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was he in turn controlled by any other individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct. He was under the control of the President, of the presidency, of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, in cooperation with the Commander of the General Staff of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After that vote was there a series of meetings between the Presidents of the Republics, Tudjman, Itzebegovic and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one such meeting held in Sarajevo at a locality called Stojcevac, I participated in the organisation, preparation and security of such a meeting which was attended by the Presidents of the former Republics of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the substance of these meetings, the topics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were discussing peaceful ways of dealing with the Yugoslav crisis. There were proposals on a confederation, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was part of the crisis the series of decisions regarding the structure and actions of the JNA during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Had the SFRY presidency declared what the purpose of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role, yes, the presidency determined the role of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was to place itself in the protection of a part of the citizens who, according to them, were in jeopardy because they did not want Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they allegedly wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina and they are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the Serb people, and in that way they said that the JNA should protect one people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: By "protect them" ------

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I rather think the transcript seems to be wrong, "... they did not want Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they allegedly wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina". There is something gone wrong in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): You said that the purpose was to protect part of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What did you mean by "protecting" those persons; what was the intent to allow those persons to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, that presidency took a decision in December '91 that the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be committed to prevent broader inter-ethnic conflicts and this could be acceptable and, secondly, it took a decision to protect the Serb people from violence and genocide which meant placing the JNA in the direct protection of one people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Which people was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb. Just before the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, in December, the presidency says that the army should first by use of force enable the peaceful resolution of the conflict, and enable all peoples in Yugoslavia who wished to live in a common state as well as those who do not wish to, to achieve that right in a peaceful way. That was the decision of the rump presidency. However, we knew what the situation was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The SDS which represented the Serb people did not want Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, if the army protects them, what about the rest of us? What protection do we have from that army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of something called the "RAM plan"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What does the word "RAM" mean in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means a frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the substance of this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The substance of the plan was to create a greater Serbia. That RAM was to follow the lines of Virovitica, Karlovac, Karlobag, which we saw confirmed in reality later on with the decision on the withdrawal of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, from Slovenia and partly from Croatia to those positions in Western Slavonia up to Karlovac and south almost to Karlobag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know where this RAM plan originated from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the RAM plan originates from the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, the so-called SANU, where it was drawn up together with the Serbian leadership, with Milosevic and some members of the General Staff of JNA -- normally in strict secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With regards to this withdrawal of JNA forces from the territory of Slovenia and then parts of Croatia, what recommendations did you make as the Minister of Defence for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding any of those forces which were coming into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, together with my associates in the Ministry, I proposed to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was later approved both there in the Assembly and by the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a proclamation that the army withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia, the JNA should go directly to Serbia and not all of them to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and only the number of troops and officers should remain in Bosnia-Herzegovina that corresponds to our economic potentialities, and those who want to have Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state and who are ready to express loyalty to the government and to the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was not accepted by the General Staff and the presidency of the Federal state at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you say the "General Staff" are you referring to the General Staff of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the General Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia presidency and the General Staff describe this relocation of forces from Slovenia and parts of Croatia? Into what territory did they describe the forces as withdrawing to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you previously through my three comments that the JNA should prevent the spreading of inter-ethnic conflicts and that it should protect inter-ethnic relations allegedly, and to protect the part of the people who wished to remain a part of former Yugoslavia, to make it possible for them to do so. You know yourself where the Serb people were living and it is to those parts that they relocated the JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What parts of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were those, that they relocated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the so-called Serb Krajinas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did this dislocation into the area referred to as the Krajina in both Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina of those JNA forces indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For us, it was an aggression against our Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there other acts by the JNA which indicated to you that there was a preparation for armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, this could be seen by the deployment of units; the control of roads by the JNA; the relocation of artillery on hill tops around all the major cities of Bosnia-Herzegovina; their collaboration with extremist forces of the SDS, arming them and assisting the arming of them; the issuance of TO weapons which were allegedly being kept in the TO storage facilities with a majority Serb population, and they did not accept our request for distribution of weapons to TO units in municipalities in which the Muslims and Croats were in a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What direct information did you receive, if any, of arming of Serbian civilians and Serbian TOs by the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, in the area of Doboj, in villages with a majority Serb population, about 8,000 automatic rifles were distributed. In the area of Foca, the armament of Serbs began already in the course of 1990, in July, on the basis of documents of the 2nd army district, and by 19th March 93 the JNA had distributed among the Serb voluntary units about 51,000 pieces of firearms and SDS members, about 23,000. These paramilitary units were also armed with some 200 tanks and only JNA had tanks. So, in all likelihood, it also gave them armoured vehicles, about 400 heavy artillery pieces, 800 mortars and so on and so forth. I could go on listing them in other areas, what they did there. They also formed four army districts directly so as to cover the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina with their structure to control it, and they also set up a large number of Corps. The Commander of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, General Adzic, visited towards the end of March '92 these troops in the area of Banja Luka and Tuzla. He visited the units of the 5th, 9th, 11th and 12th Corps of the JNA to check their combat preparedness for the forthcoming combat operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He came there. We, I mean my Ministry and my Prime Minister, were not even informed of this visit, even though we knew that he was coming. Then there was a Corps and those JNA units had -- if these Corps and JNA units were to protect Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would be natural for that Commander of these forces from Belgrade to inform us about that and co-operate with us. Evidently, their intentions were quite different, as they demonstrated later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This inspection trip by General Adzic of the JNA General Staff, was there a request by the Republic presidency to accompany him, as was required under prior law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The presidency requested immediately from them not to come to Bosnia-Herzegovina without the knowledge of the presidency, without the approval of the presidency, but obviously they paid no attention to the decisions and requests of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were doing their job, the job as they have conceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you receive any direct reports from General Vukosavljevic, the Commander of the TO in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, about the arming of Serbs by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at a session of the presidency, of the enlarged presidency, when the JNA had already occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had no possibility to move out, to leave Sarajevo, members of the government and the presidency; but we maintained contact with our people in their field and they informed us that those TO units were supplied with weapons in Sipovo and Mrkonjic Grad, and members of the enlarged presidency under wartime conditions were Minister of Defence and Minister of the Interior, the Foreign Minister, the Prime Minister and the Chairman of the TO staff. General Vukosavljevic then told us that he knew nothing about it. When we asked him: "Well, who should know that?" he said that he should know it and nothing should be done without him, and that he could receive orders about such operations only from the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The next day he said he would notify us about it, and then said something completely different. He said that that was all right, that it was approved by the Commander of the Banja Luka Corps commanded by General Nikola Uzelac, and that he gave them weapons and that that was in line with some kind of a military order which we could not accept because it was anti-constitutional act and an act against legality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did General Vukosavljevic leave his position as the Commander of the TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He fled on 5th April '92. He attended a meeting with us the day before that -- the meeting that I have just told you about. He fled to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you at a later time go to the offices of the TO for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 6th April we entered the premises which were locked so we had to break in. We found no records because they had all been taken away by his associates and people who stayed behind and those who stated their loyalty from the staff, as I have already said, at the beginning, the commanders, deputies and for individual offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Returning to the time after the inspection trip by General Adzic, what was the state of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina and was there reinforcement of the forces there during that time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were reinforcements. According to the information, '92, the JNA troops deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina were about 100,000 armed soldiers, I mean soldiers and officers; about 700 to 800 tanks were there; 1,000 APCs and other armoured vehicles; over 4,000 mortars and artillery pieces; up to 100 aircraft and 500 helicopters which meant large concentration of strength and weapon materiel and equipment in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and at the same time JNA occupied that Republic with these troops and armaments were under direct command of the General Staff of the JNA and, to our knowledge, it was already under a major influence, under major sway, of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After May 19th 1992 when there was a public division of the JNA, with the renaming of those forces in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the army of Republika Srpska, what type of men and equipment were left to form that army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all the types of armaments that I have just listed. The Yugoslav People's Army left behind all weapons to that so-called army, Serb army, the army of the Serb -- of the Serb Republic, because it had none, just as we had none. We all, all peoples of that Republic, paid for those weapons and yet it fell into the hands of only one people and the armed force, as they called it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When was the first act of direct aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina by troops of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may have a look at this? The aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serbian Montenegrin aggressor took place on 20th September 1991. That was when the JNA troops from the Uzice Drava Corps claiming that the army airfield in Mostar and the Serb population in East Herzegovina were in danger, and the real excuse was the preparation for the Dubrovnik/Split operation within the “RAM” plan. They erupted the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Serbia Montenegro. These Corps were filled up with large numbers of reserves and volunteers from Serbia and Herzegovina who embarked on unprecedented terror against non-Serb population, plundering of property, persecution of the population. As of 1991, those troops participated in the attack on the village of Ravno and mostly inhabited by Croats. They killed a number of villagers and destroyed the village claiming that paramilitary units of the Republic of Croatia had fired at JNA units. The real truth is that several soldiers of these troops were killed in an ambush near a village, Cepikuce, which is in the territory of Croatia. On 10th April, these units shelled Dubrave in the municipality of Stolac and conducted operations above Neum and Podvelezje in Mostar. On 9th April they took tactical positions around Doboj, took over Modrica and continued to deploy their troops between Tuzla and Gracanica. On April 12th they entered the towns of Mesici and Ustipraca and captured Jabuka. During the night of April 13th, they took positions north east of Mostar and blocked the south, an area of the town. On April 16th, they came out to Mojmil Brdo and Dobrinja, near Sarajevo, and the Yugoslav People's Army and the armed SDS formations surrounded Brcko and the broader area around Gurbavica on April 17th -- Gradacac, excuse me, on April 17th. In the night of April 20th, the armoured mechanized units of the JNA blockaded Vlasenica, a town which, according to '91 census, 55.3 per cent of the population were Bosniaks, Muslims, and 42.2 per cent Serbs, and helped that the power of the city be seized by the so-called Serb guard and the SDS. On April 25th, JNA tanks entered Bratunac and together with SDS armoured groups committed a mass crime against the Muslims -- against the Bosniaks. On April 28th '92, JNA artillery destroyed Tomislavgrad and its engineers destroyed the bridge across the Sava at Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Doko, you indicated that initial troops involved were the Uzice and Podgorica Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where is Uzice located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uzice is in Serbia, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where is Podgorica located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the capital of the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How do you know that this particular invasion on 20th September 1991 occurred in that location and with those units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 21st September, when they reached the elevation above the Stolac municipality, I agreed with some members of the government to go to this site and see where that army had come from and why had they come to that piece of land. I requested from the Mostar garrison Commander and his Deputy, Slobodan Pudar, Lieutenant Colonel, to come with us and see, because I had asked them whether they knew who that was, and what it was all about, and they had said that they did not know. So they came with me and I recognised the army. I even recognised a lad, a young man, from the Republic of Montenegro, from a place called Bar, who was with those units. They were wearing different uniforms from JNA to TO uniforms. Some of them even had the Chetnik fur caps. When I asked that young man why had he come there, what was his intention, he said that that was Serb land and that Serbia extended as far as that. We advised the government which had sent them there. That is how we learned what units those were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated in your prior testimony the Podgrica Corps remained on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina through a large part of 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he stayed there. It is a fact that the units which came to Mostar to supposedly guard the Mostar airfield committed a massacre on 18th June 92 at a place called Uborak and Sutina on the outskirts of Mostar where 88 bodies of Muslims and Croats were found with their throats slit and killed and another 12 at a place called Sutina. At the time they were commanded by General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the Podgrica Corps also involved in the conflict in the area of Trebinje in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the summer and fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I could have this document marked number 180? If that could be placed on the elmo? (To the witness): Mr. Doko, Exhibit 180 is the English translation of an article which appeared in the Belgrade Tanjug, domestic service, regarding the denial by the Podgrica Corps of its withdrawal from the Prevlaka Peninsular on 28th September 1992. Are you familiar with this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this article and with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would tender Exhibit 180.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 180 will be admitted. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Is Tanjug the state controlled news agency for Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This article indicates that it is a statement by the 2nd army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia army, the information service. Is that the official information service for the army? I will repeat the question. The article indicates that it has been released by the 2nd army's information service; the 2nd army being part of the Yugoslav Army. Is that the official information service for the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tanjug is not an official information service for the army; it is an official state agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I am talking about the article itself which indicates it is released, the article was released, to Tanjug by the 2nd army's information service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The article states, "The members of the Yugoslav's Army's Podgrica Corps deployed east of Dubrovnik are carrying out their regular tasks in line with the commanding body's orders", and indicates it has no intention of withdrawing from the area. What area is east of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trebinje in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was, in fact, the Podgrica Corps of what was then called the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Yugoslav Army still engaged in armed conflict in the Trebinje area in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned earlier General Perisic. Who was General Perisic and what unit was he commanding in late 1991, the time frame you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the end of '91 he came to command the JNA garrison in Mostar from Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What attacks was he responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean when he came to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was responsible for attacks for the destruction, demolition of bridges on the Neretva River; the massacre I have just described in Mostar, Uborak and Sutina; killing of civilians in Mostar, demolition of the town. He led those operations directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In February or March 1992, did you have a conversation with General Perisic regarding the attack on Mostar and Zadar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did. As I am from Mostar, and it was my duty as I was Minister for Defence, I did go to Mostar to his office in the northern section of Mostar. We discussed it at length, and he said that they had deceived him in Zadar -- I saw Zadar after his departure, what it was like, how destroyed it was -- and that he would destroy it, that he would raise it to the ground. I tried to talk to him as a normal man, and I realised it was a no-go, and then I realised that he would destroy Mostar, that he would commit all those misdeeds. I realised what the orders he was given for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: OK. You said that he told you they had deceived him in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did that statement mean to you, what was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it meant that he was not a normal man, and that Mostar would fair even worse because it was impossible to communicate, to talk with him, normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I am referring to the statement, "they deceived me". Who was the "they" that General Perisic was referring to and why did he feel deceived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was deceived by his superiors who had said that Zadar would be part of greater Serbia and when nothing came out with the withdrawal to the retreat to Neretva, and then he said that the Serbian border would be on the Neretva and that he would not be deceived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What position did General Perisic later take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was rewarded by becoming the Commander of the military district in Nis. Shortly after that, he took up the highest ranking position, that is, the Commander of the Chief of the armed forces of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that might be a convenient time before we start a new topic?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (4.00 p.m.) (Adjourned for a short time) (4.20 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Doko, after the initial shelling attack of Sarajevo in April 1992, did you have any direct contact with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the nature of that contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you receive that telephone call, can you describe the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the previous night was the first shelling with rocket fire of Sarajevo, so that in the building of the presidency where I was, members of the presidency and other members of the government, we recorded the command of General Mladic and we followed it. The next day we had a tape where he is speaking to his artillery command, asking them: "Do you have the presidency under fire? Nikola, are you ready? Hit the presidency", and then we hear the rocket. That night there were injured people, one of my secretary from the Ministry was injured, the water, the gas supply ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you speak to General Mladic yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and the presidency was hit. After such a situation in the building, I came to work normally at 8 o'clock in the morning, the other workers were not there yet, and thinking, and my thinking in the office was interrupted by the ringing of the telephone. When I lifted the receiver, a voice asked: "Is that Minister Doko?" I said: "Who is speaking?" and the voice said: "General Mladic." At first I did not want to believe it. I said I did not like to joke with such things especially after such a night. He said: "It is me". I recognised his voice because I had spoken to him earlier on when we were emptying the barracks in the city of Sarajevo. I recognised his voice and he said, among other things: "I have called you to let you know I have 110 tubes targeting you and Sarajevo, I will kill you all". I answered that he cannot do anything to us, that we have a heart and the people will rise against him and that he cannot destroy all the people and the city of Sarajevo. That was the conversation I had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
