utterances.text: Do you have any direct knowledge of involvement of paramilitary forces led by an individual known as Arkan in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Zeljko Raznjetovic, Arkan, at the end of March '92 entered Bijeljina and committed a massacre in Bijeljina. He killed civilians. We watched that on the media, on television. Then we convened a session of the presidency at which a decision was taken that a delegation on behalf of the presidency and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina should go to Bijeljina to see what is happening there. It was decided that Fikret Abdic should go on behalf of the presidency and the Vice Prime Minister, Simovic, on behalf of the government and myself as Defence Minister. We started on our journey. We arrived late at night outside of Bijeljina. We were stopped there by some armed formations with black masks over their heads. They said they were Arkan units and that we could not go to Bijeljina. In the meantime, some other soldiers approached us. They insulted us. They swore at us, calling us "Turks", "Ustashas". They told us to lie on the ground, to lie down. This lasted for a couple of minutes, and one of them with a black mask had a mobile radio station, a Motorola, and as he was close to me I heard a voice at the other end asking: "Are the guests there?" implying us, members of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When he answered "yes", he said that he must not hurt us and the soldiers left. They told us to get up. We waited for about 40 minutes, then Zeljko Raznjetovic Arkan came in person. He introduced himself. He was accompanied by five of his soldiers. When we told him that we wanted to talk to him about what was happening in Bijeljina, he said that Bijeljina was Serb, that it was his, that he had come with his fighters to Bijeljina and there was nothing to talk about. When Mr. Abdic insisted on a talk, this was on Tuesday, then he said that they should come on Saturday when everything was settled. Then we returned after midnight via Brcko, Tuzla to Sarajevo; and on that Saturday Mr. Abdic together with Biljana Plavsic went to Bijeljina, and you know the photographs showing her kissing Arkan in the centre of Bijeljina. That was my encounter with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This second delegation that was sent, you said that Biljana Plavsic was one of the members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second delegation that went after us on Saturday consisted of Fikret Abdic and Biljana Plavsic, members of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. They went to Bijeljina. They could enter Bijeljina; we could not. They entered and at the square -- this was shown on television -- everyone saw her kissing Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the common interpretation of her greeting of Arkan in the square by kissing him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Biljana Plavsic is a member of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time and the Vice President, and she is Vice President of SDS, the Vice President of Karadzic; and the people thought that these were criminals who were killing our people, they were occupiers and aggressors and, therefore, this greeting by kissing was considered approval and acceptance of them by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No cross-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you were asked about a telephone conversation that you had with General Mladic, you began by describing a conversation that, I gather, you intercepted in some way. Did you have means to intercept the conversation between General Mladic and the people in control of the artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Let me explain perhaps: as I understood your evidence, when you were being shelled in the presidency building, you heard, you overheard, a conversation between General Mladic and somebody who was operating the guns; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You did not, however, explain how you overheard that. Was that because you had some method of intercepting the radio communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had links between our staff and their staff, and the next day, and after five days the whole world had this tape translated into five languages where you hear the orders saying, "Nikola, do you have the presidency targeted? Now fire", and this was published, this tape was heard, in the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have no additional questions. Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Defence, cross-examination, any?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Mr. Doko being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Doko, you are permanently excused. Thank you for coming. You may leave now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would call Mr. Ed Vulliamy next. MR. ED VULLIAMY, called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since the court has indicated some interest in some advance notice of where we are going, just for the court's information, this is at this time intended to be the last policy witness in the case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be given an oath to take in a moment, if it is there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Edward Sebastian Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you are a citizen of the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you attend university and what was your major area of studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at university at Oxford in England and thereafter at Florence in Italy studying politics and philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you become a journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What organisation do you currently work for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment I am employed by The Guardian of London.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What areas of interest do you generally cover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All sorts of things, although latterly I have been overwhelmingly involved by the war in the former Yugoslavia, and I have covered over conflicts elsewhere in the world for The Guardian and other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What particular awards have you received as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I won a thing called the Royal Television Society Award for Current Affairs in the mid 1980s for a film I made about Northern Ireland, and for my work in the former Yugoslavia I won a thing called the Granada Television International Reporter of the Year Award; in the British Press Awards, Foreign Correspondent of the Year award; I won an award presented by Amnesty International described as "For Journalism in the interests of Human Rights" and then I won a thing called the James Cameron prize which is referred to as the sort of British Pulitzer, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In addition to reporting on the war for The Guardian and other publications, are you also the author of a book titled "Seasons in Hell" which is about the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and your experiences there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Sir, when did you first begin to cover the story of the break up of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right at the beginning. I was based in Rome and was sent to Slovenia right at the start in the summer of 1991 during the first exchanges between the fairly ad hoc Slovene army and the Yugoslav People's Army in that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did you first travel to the former Yugoslavia to cover the conflict directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What area did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I started off in Eastern Slovenia, in Ljubljiana, the capital of Slovenia. Then the war progressed into Croatia and in Croatia I was, well, all over the place actually, based in Zagreb most of the time and travelling out for periods ranging from one day to a week or maybe even two weeks to the area south of Zagreb which was a confrontation line between the Croatian Serbs and the Croatian government -- nascent Croatian government. I worked a lot in the Eastern Slavonia area around Vukovar, Vinkovci and Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this document marked as the next exhibit which will be 181 and then shown to the witness, please? Your Honour, I would tender Exhibit 181.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 181 will be admitted. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): For your information, that is a map that was previously provided. Mr. Vulliamy, if you could ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Start again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- indicate on the map where you started your direct coverage of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, I began here in Slovenia, in this area, and going off the map up here, and then the war moved to Croatia. I was based in the capital area, in Zagreb. I worked a lot around this part, Glina, Petrinja, Sisak. That was a confrontation line between or, as it was then, emergent confrontation line between the Croatian Serbs and the Croatian forces, such as they were then. I spent a lot of time in this area here, Vukovar, Borovo, Delj, Osijek, Vinkovci and around these front lines where the siege of Vukovar was later laid. Working on both sides, we used to go up through Hungary and then down into Eastern Serbia, Sombor, Apatin, Bogojevo (is a place that is not marked on the map, an important town), an important town called Sid here near Vukovar. So I was working on the Serbian side or the Yugoslav side, as it most properly would be described at that time, and the Croatian side and also later during the siege of Dubrovnik, down here on the coast -- it is down here -- when the Montenegrin forces, as they were then, were laying siege to Dubrovnik; so pretty much across the whole Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could return to the Vinkovci/Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is here in the eastern part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Approximately what time frame was that that you were covering that aspect of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first went to that area when one could still cross between the two communities, cross the lines as they later became, in the summer, in July or late June of 1991, and continued there right until towards the end of the war and the collapse of Vukovar in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the types of forces that were involved on both sides and the type of weaponry which they had arrayed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. On the Croatian side, you had fairly sort of scratched together army, motivated but scantily armed at first, progressively slightly better armed as the war went on. They were defending Vukovar where I was until the day before the Vukovar was cut off by the Serbs and completely surrounded. We came out through a track through a cornfield under fire on the penultimate day that Vukovar was still open. Then the Croatian armies were based mostly in Osijek which is there and Vinkovci, using kalashnikov rifles, they had the odd sort of make-shift tank. They would make armoured vehicles themselves out of cars sometimes. On the Serbian side or the Yugoslav People's Army side, it was an altogether different picture. I spent a lot of time in the militarized towns of Bogojevo, which is in western Serbia, about here just near the Croatian border, and at this important town of Sid, there near Vukovar. These were barrack towns, effectively, where large collections of tanks and armoured vehicles were being collected and accumulated, repaired. Men were clearly billeted there. If men were fighting in Croatian territory, they might retire there for the evening, because the distances are short, for a drink or so. The pattern there was quite easily discernible. It was a question of front lines which were in the main held by irregulars local to the villages within Croatia, the Serbian villages within the Croatian side, backed up by large rows of tanks and artillery which were on a fairly persistent basis coming across the border from these garrison towns of Bogojevo and Sid. We used to follow that movement and report it quite carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you have contact with these "irregulars", as you called them, paramilitaries, and discuss with them their role in that conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, very much so, over and over again -- ad nauseam, it felt like sometimes. We would spend a lot of time on the front lines with them. We would have a drink with them in the bars after work, if that is the right expression. We used to spend nights out with them or I used to spend nights out with them on their front lines sometimes, most especially at a place called Bijelo Brdo which is within Croatia, just over the border with Serbia. I had a particularly illuminating night out with the regulars on the front of the front line. It was literally in a house and the Croats were in the houses on the other side of the field, and they were having a hell of an exchange across the field. And, yes, I talked to them about the war, their lives, what they thought they were doing and they were pretty clear about what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did they see as their role there? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, best described, perhaps, by one chap who struck his hand across a table and just went "to Zagreb", zoom, like that. (Indicating) That was anecdotal and he had a few drinks, I admit, but that seemed to be the general idea. Yes, we talked to them a lot in a place called Borovo Selo which was the irregulars' base, I suppose, within Croatia. Yes, they were up front about it. They did not make any secret. We talked tactics with them as well specifically, I mean, about how they were going to surround Osijek and take it from behind, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you observe in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Borovo Selo was one of the important crossroads or meeting points between the regular soldiers from the Yugoslav People's Army and the irregulars fighting on the front of the front lines. It was a strategically important place because it was the last Serbian village before Vukovar, which the Croats still held, and it was also one of the places from which artillery and tanks and men could fan out on to the various points to which they were ordered on the front lines themselves. So -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Where is that? Could you locate that, sir, on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. You can see on the map "Borovo" just there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hate to sound too complicated, but Borovo is actually Croat. Borovo Selo, which means Borovo village literally, is the older part of the habitation, just to the north of Borovo there on the map. So the line, the front line, was between Borovo and Borovo Selo; the Serbian bit being just to the north of the bit marked "Borovo" on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From what you observed, was there clear coordination between these paramilitary or volunteer groups and the organised JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, undoubtedly. They were socializing together, and in the barracks in Bogojevo and in Sid, you would see them sharing quarters, sharing yards where their equipment would be parked. The Yugoslav Army officers whom I interviewed and spoke to and spent a lot of time with were quite clear that they were in charge of both their own regular forces and the people that they were, as it were, servicing on the ground in the villages where they were fighting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you observe that coordination and control on the battlefield as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was no secret about it. I referred to a night I spent on the front line at this place, Bijelo Brdo, and the pattern there was these houses on the edge of the field, with the irregulars and snipers firing at the Croats on the other side of the field, and in the field indeed, and behind them were these tanks parked in the widest street in the village pointing towards Osijek, the Croat town, and the Croatian lines. So, it was co-ordinated. It was fairly straightforward and it made sense. Similarly, at a place called Trpinje which is in the Vukovar area, we had again small houses full of irregulars and snipers and people talking on the radio, indeed talking into Vukovar sometimes to people they knew and to whom they were laying siege ironically, and they would then be serviced from behind by a large row of mortars manned by soldiers from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In addition to that, after that conflict in the Vukovar/Vinkovci area, did you go on to cover the war in former Yugoslavia on a continuous basis in other areas -- and in other areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did after -- I mean, the Vukovar area was one that one returned to over and over again. Then eventually that war came to an end, a temporary end, and things were just starting up in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you then travel to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had been to Bosnia, in fact, before the start of the war because one of the Colonels of the JNA I had got to -- the Yugoslav People's Army -- that I had got to know in the Croatian war was starting opening up a front fighting into Croatia, so that was the first time I went to Bosnia and then, indeed, I was dispatched back to cover the war as it broke out in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you quickly point out on the map the various places in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other areas in the former Yugoslavia that you visited since 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, forgive me if I take some time on this because the answer is, most of it. I will do it geographically rather than chronologically, if you like. Well, here is the Bihac pocket. That was under siege by the Serbs. It is a Muslim area. I worked in there. Here is the Bosnian Krajina area, as it called, around Prijedor and Banja Luka. I worked there. This is all, by the way, between 1992 and up until only a few weeks ago. I worked in the capital, Sarajevo, under siege. I worked a great deal in this area here, central Bosnia we will call it, Turbe, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Zenica, Vitez. All these places I know well, very well. I worked in Herzegovina which is the area down here to the southeast, mainly Croat, most especially in Mostar here, the capital of Herzegovina. I worked in Tuzla which is -- here it is, up here, in that area, upper central Bosnia, let us say. Latterly, because it was closed off during the war, but during the period just after the war I began to explore the Drina valley area around here, Visegrad, Rogatica and the Serbian held territory around here. So, I suppose the answer has to be, most of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In all of those locations did you speak with members of all three main ethnic or national groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely -- at great length.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you speak with military, police and paramilitary members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In all of those conversations, did you focus on their role in the conflict, how they were conducting it, or how they had been victimized, its origins and its purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, whether they were the victims or the perpetrators or the officers or the troops or whoever they were, we talked about little else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In your research and reporting on the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly in 1992, and in the research for your book, did you speak with fellow journalists and review archive records about events that were occurring in different regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as regards the fellow journalists, I mean, as you can imagine, we were quite a clan and used to compare notes obsessively all the time, every day, every night that we were there. As regards historical records and archives, yes, I mean, certainly for the book, I would read all the books that seemed to be necessary and many that were not out of interest and as much source material as I could, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did some of that source material include official reports by government and non-governmental agencies and organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all sorts of stuff from all the governments involved and through non-government agencies -- you mean within the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct, such as the ICRC, UNHCR etc.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely, yes. We used to read all their stuff, talk to the UNHCR, talk to the Red Cross, share information with them, get information from them and, more often than not, actually give them information because there were places that we could get to that they could not, so it is not one-way traffic, it is multi-way traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With regard to people of Serbian descent, particularly those in what are known as the Krajina regions, both in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as just over the border in the Republic of Serbia, based on your experiences and your conversations, did you determine that there was a difference in their perspective toward people that were considered to be Muslims as compared to people who were considered to be of Croatian descent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbs in the Bosnian Krajina and the Croatian Krajina certainly regarded both these people as their foe, but in a different way. I always felt, especially during the war in Croatia, that the Serbs and the Croats opposed but respected each other. They feared each other. The Serbs were in awe of the Croats, as well they might have been given the history that they had and past generation of the Second World War. So there was a sort of mutual respect, if you like, between two powerful peoples, two proud peoples. The view of the Muslims by the Serbs in that region was a different one. Very occasionally they would be referred as mad Islamic fanatics or fundamentalists or something, which is water off my back I have to say, but more often it was far more disparaging. They would be termed "balija" which is common word and translates roughly as filthy gypsy. There was no fear of these people beyond a rather sort of camped up propaganda line. They were considered dirty, all the usual sort of epithets that one hears about too many people in the world, breed like rabbits, that sort of thing. When I was with a convoy of Muslims being ethnically cleansed, being herded over the mountains at gunpoint once, some people were shouting at us from the side of the road, I think, I have will to check, but it is "zakalati tocu vas" or something like that, and I asked my Serbo-Croat speaking friend what that meant and he said, oh, it means "butcher them, butcher them" but is the language, it is the word we use to describe animal slaughter, not human beings. That was the tenor of the thing, these people were dirty gypsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you notice this type of description about the Muslims by the Serbian leaders in the discussions with you and in the press or in their speeches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. A conversation comes to mind of the Vice President of the now Republika Srpska, a man called Nikola Koljevic, a professor, who would talk about Muslims, they are uneducated, they are dirty, they do not understand these things, they have no history. He used the term once "racial memory", he said they have no racial memory. They are not a people, he said, "narod" is the term, in the sense of rather like the German Volk. Yes, this constant allusion to them being dirty, having too many children, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you see the use of propaganda by the Serb leaders in your experience to condition the Serbian people and fighters at the start of and throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The message from the government in Belgrade and its sort of sub-governments on the ground in Bosnia was a fairly relentless one, on television, in press statements, at meetings that one might attend. Most of us, when I say "us" I mean journalists and aid workers and so on, would think of it as banal, but it was certainly very cogent and potent. It was a message of urgency, a threat to your people, to your nation, a call to arms, and, yes, a sort of an instruction to go to war for your people. This came through in all sorts of way, some through cartoons, through magazines, through television, but it was relentless. It pushed and pushed. It was rather like a sort of hammer bashing on peoples' heads I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, if I could, your testimony still has to be translated both into French and Serbia Croatian, so if could I ask you to slow down a bit in your speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In your research both for your articles and for your book, did you determine whether there was an historical precedent for the use of propaganda and paramilitaries officially associated with the Regular Army to commit atrocities to further a Serbian cause?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely, yes. During research for the book I went into the histories of the Serbian revolt against the Ottoman Empire, the Serbian revolt against Austro-Hungarian rule, and above all the emergence of what we might call the modern Serbian extremist nationalist movement in the Second World War, and each time there was a pattern of the army, be it the Royal Army or the Yugoslav Army or a self-appointed Serbian army, co-operating with and using irregulars. They used to call them all sorts of things, but "Cheta" was the word that started to emerge, the band from which the word "Chetnik" comes now used to describe the Serbian royalist strictly and, more broadly, the nationalist movement. But, yes, it was a recurrent theme throughout the history of the people and their country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you find a similarity between the type of propaganda used back then and the use of the paramilitaries during that time with the propaganda during the current conflict and how paramilitaries were used in the current conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The language echoed down the decades, if not the centuries, certainly. That is the theme that dominated the war, was that this was constantly a reactivation, a re-enactment of the past, and that language did resound at all these instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Based on your research and your extensive contact with Serbs from all walks of life, in your opinion are the Serbs a people who are both literate in and motivated by their history?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I think it is worth saying that when we say "Serbs", if I could just make this clear, there were Serbs who fought in this struggle, this war, against the Muslims and the Croats and those who did not. There are very large numbers of Serbs who stayed in Sarajevo who could have left and did not and large numbers who fought for the government side that we often like to call the Muslim side. One kept meeting Serbs. My translator in Sarajevo who was under siege and her brother was in the army, she was a Serb and she was fighting the other side. So when we say "Serbs" I do not mean all Serbs. So let us say the Serbs who accepted the language, if you like, the call to arms that had come from Belgrade and from Banja Luka and Pale, they indeed showed not just an awareness of this history, but I would say obsession with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In your opinion were the leaders of the Serbian peoples both in the Serbian Republic and in the Krajina areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia aware of both the historical precedent and the obsession, as you put it, with the Serbian history among the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely. I mean the leader I came into contact with most personally was Professor Koljevic who I mentioned before, the Vice President of Dr. Karadzic, now Vice President of Republika Srpska, and, yes, I interviewed him only a matter of weeks ago and he was talking about racial memory being a thing that was most important to the Serbs. He said that: "This war that we have just been fighting is the third great Balkan war." He was a leader, he was the No. 2. Everything that was happening was being set in the historical context, was part of history, was a continuation of history. So he was certainly obsessed by history, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there particular documents or writings which were relied upon by the Serbian leaders in promoting their ideals and these historical arguments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, yes, there were various tracks from the 1940s which were reproduced, regurgitated and quoted in some of the soldiers' manuals which used to talk about a greater Serbia whose frontiers varied on whatever year you were talking about, but seemed to engulf most of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if not all, and large chunks of Croatia. They were from the 40s, from the Second World War. Then there would be more recent texts like a memorandum from a group called the SANU, the Academy of Sciences in Belgrade who resurrected this idea of the greater Serbia and wrote a famous or infamous memorandum urging its reconstruction, and that was certainly a document that would be quoted from. There were other epic poems and cultural points of reference that would crop up. But, yes, there are texts and they are well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the SANU memorandum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I read it. I cannot remember it that well, but I remember its gist. It was produced in Belgrade. It was supposed to be, if you like, the "think tank" of the new thinking in Serbia at the time, spear headed by President Milosevic. Yes, it called for a resurrection of the greater Serbia, for a renaissance amongst the Serbian people in the sense of ethnic pride, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the contents of these various memorandums or the gist of their arguments regularly published and republished in papers and periodicals and discussed on the radio and TV in the Serbian areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in various forms they were and also by their opponents of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned your direct involvement with some paramilitary and volunteer forces in Croatia in 1991. Did you have any direct contact with volunteer forces or paramilitary forces from the Republic of Serbia in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the second half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was one occasion I recall when I was in Prijedor police station waiting for papers to carry further on down the road, this was in late August 1992, and we chanced upon a band of pretty rugged individuals who were among the few who called themselves Chetnik without apology. They told us that they had been fighting down in a place called Klucj which was further south of a town in which there had been a large number of Muslims now held by the Serbs, and they were telling us that they had been down there and they were on their way back to Serbia. One was from a place called Nis that I was talking to which is a large industrial town in the south of Serbia. They seemed to be either taking a meal at, if not barracked at, the police station, but then the local police did not want us to carry on this conversation; they asked to go and wait in another room. That was one encounter I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you happen to see what type of transportation they were using to move around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Large military coloured buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the markings on those buses or trucks from Serbia, the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You say you ran across them in the police station in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in police station there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did it appear that they were there as a result of any sort of legal action or apprehension or did it appear they were there as guests, if you will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were using the police station as some sort of resting place or billet. I got the impression they were passing through. They were, as they said themselves, on their way home after a few days tour almost. Yes, I got the impression that on their way back if they needed to stop the police station was the obvious place to go and they were welcome there. As I recall they were sort of half known there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Having followed the breakup of the former Yugoslavia from the beginning, are you aware that there were periodic statements about crisis involving refugees and the Commission of Atrocities from UN agencies, the ICRC, both Herzegovina papers and Serbian papers, as well as statements by political and military leaders from all of the Republics in the former Yugoslavia, as well as Bosnian-Croat and Bosnian-Serb officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was outside the territory of the former Yugoslavia for the first, for most of the first two months of the war, that is to say April/May 1992, but glued to the papers, glued to the television. Obviously I was following everything that the UNHCR, the Refugee Commission was saying and the Red Cross and the leaders and the Croatian Government too who were responsible for most of the refugees coming into their territory. So, yes, I was following it carefully and following the statements that the UNHCR, in particular, were making about very large numbers of people. At one a Mr. Kesler of UNHCR said it was the worst exodus or forced movement of people since the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you were in fact, that you took part in a convoy of refugees. Can you describe how that came about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were in Zagreb and the UNHCR had just decided with the Croatian Government, well, the Croatian Government had said that they just could not take any more of these refugees; they had been pouring across the border from northern Bosnia and they could not take any more. The UNHCR at the same time decided that they were not going, as it were, to play the game by accepting these people longer. We were sitting in Zagreb, a friend of mine and I, and we said, well, there is the front door shut, that will not stop what is going on; I wonder where the back door is. It dawned on us -- in fact he said, well, there is only one way to find out, isn't there? Yes, I know, we have got to go and get ethnically cleansed ourselves. So we did. We went down into the Prijedor area and stumbled upon a great convoy parked along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the map where it was you came across this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prijedor here. It was just a little outside Prijedor, between Prijedor and Kozarac there. There is a little hamlet there called Lamovita which is where it was exactly, but it is just a few miles east of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When was this Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is late August 1992. I believe August 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Approximately how big was this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We counted them. There were 55 cars and 11 to 15 trucks, and six to eight buses jam packed with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you determine where this convoy had originated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We, they were parked up on the road and we thought, well, here it is, let's slip in, so we did. They were having a break, so we started talking to people and they had come from a place called Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could indicate, please, on the map where that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is just there. It is now marked as part of the Muslim Croat Federation territory but was then in Serbian hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you determine the ethnic background of the people, the refugees on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim, one or two Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you determine that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just asked them. It did not take much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there any official forces accompanying this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were being escorted, one might say, herded would be more accurate, by the Bosnian-Serb police in blue uniforms and carrying Kalashnikov guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you joined the convoy in Lamovita -- I am sorry, did you determine how many people were on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was hard to establish immediately, but our calculations coupled with their accounts came out at about 1600.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did the individuals on that convoy indicate to you this convoy had been started or organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they told us exactly what had happened to them that morning. They had been told to come out of their homes. An announcement on the local radio taken over by the Serbs the previous day had said that this was the last chance for the Muslims, assemble tomorrow morning, the transport for those of you who do not have cars we will take you, bring your own car if you want to. They would have to pay to go. As the journey proceeded they told us what had been happening to them in Sanski Most; before departure they were under attack in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you where they were supposed to be going on this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had been told that they were going to Germany or Austria and that all the papers had been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the route that the convoy actually took by showing it on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We went down this road through Banja Luka, and a little after Banja Luka started climbing up into the mountains on tiny little tracks and around river gorges and over the tops of mountains and mountain tops. The route we would take was through this place called Skender Vakuf which is a small town up in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe what occurred in Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Skender Vakuf was the last town on anything resembling tarmac, and it was quite a frightening place; everybody there was military or paramilitary. They would stop the cars every now and then as they pleased, they were fairly drunk most of them, and they would perhaps open the door spit and kick or they would smash a window. They stopped our car and it was quite frightening because a man was shouting at me and I thought that if I let on that I was a foreigner there was no guarantee of my safety at all. So I feigned deaf and dumb and my friend who spoke the language said, "There's no point in talking to him, he can't understand a word you are saying." They gave me a Chinese burn, took the windscreen wiper off, kicked the car and sent us on our way, but I think others had worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After Sanski Most what was the next stop you made on that route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Skender Vakuf we went up into the mountains. We had no idea where we were going and they kept stopping the convoy at various installations, factories and sort of industrial farm buildings like hen coops and things which seemed empty. It was a little worrying because we thought maybe this the destination, what happens if it is a camp, where are we going, we do not know. So we stopped and started and stopped and started. Observations I recall, important ones, would have been, one, this was a rare opportunity to see the artillery atop the hills and there was a lot of guns, howitzer guns, canons, rocket launches, all sorts of things and a quite remarkable amount of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you made these stops at these various locations, did you talk to the refugees who were in the vehicles and in the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we would sit out on the grass and they used to give us some cheese and something like that and we would talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were their concerns when you stopped at these various locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, nobody knew where we were going. We said, "Is this a camp?" At one point somebody said, "I hope this is not a massacre". My friend said: "I think the unspeakable has just been spoken." So no one had any idea what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were people taken out of the convoy by either the police or the military personnel in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we carried on. It was getting towards dusk, it was getting quite frightening. We went through a place called Vitovje which is south of Skender Vakuf, and we saw some girls being taken from a red car towards the rear of the convoy. We had stopped by then. There was a row, there was an argument, people getting very excited. We were not quite clear what was going on. I admit now that we were too stupid then to realise what was going on. One subsequently developed a fairly clear idea about why two girls would be taken prisoner from a car. But, yes, women were being taken from the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were those women returned to the vehicle before the convoy moved on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that also the place where the people were yelling at the convoy, "Butcher them, butcher them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slaughter them, slaughter them, yes. They literally came streaming across the meadows spitting at us, shouting at us, going like that with their hands across their throats, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were some vehicles also stolen from the convoy at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a little later when we got to the last Serbian line by which time dark had fallen and, yes, all the vehicles were taken, except six. The people were simply evicted from the cars, told to take whatever they could manage on foot, and all the people on the buses were taken off the buses. Trucks were confiscated too and the cars systematically turned around back to from whence we had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where was this that this occurred, the final end of the ride?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time it was the middle of absolutely nowhere and the dead of night. It became pretty clear what it was, if not where. We were being sent out along a road towards the No Man's Land and ultimately towards the frontline of the outside, the Muslim-Croat line. This was very frightening because rule one in war is never cross lines and for all we knew we would be the first such procession of our kind, and that any sensible soldier on the other side seeing us coming would probably open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there a name to this village that was at the end of the Serbian line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was called Smet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who were the people that were controlling this line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They looked like irregular soldiers inasmuch as they were armed quite well, but they were dressed in a mixture of casual clothes and fatigues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At this point in this village of Smet all of the people from the convoy were disgorged from the vehicles and the buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all except for six cars that were allowed through one of which was ours. That was the point at which we revealed ourselves as journalists and they allowed us to keep the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the police who were escorting the convoy say anything to the people or give them any indication as to what was to lay in store?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They just set them out along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that all of the vehicles had turned round and left. Who took the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers, the men with the guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At that village were people also forced to turn over all valuables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That had happened just earlier. During a stop a bus broke down just in front of us and soldiers came down the line of cars. They were taking petrol. I saw a woman having her ring taken and possessions that the soldiers liked the look of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As you passed through the line, was there any military activity going on, any firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a lot. The fire was coming over our heads mostly. There was a village held by the Muslims and the Croats down in the valley about a quarter of a mile beneath us, and the fires coming over our heads and a lot of it was tracer fire so you could see it quite clearly. Yes, there was a lot of fighting on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see any indications that people had been recently killed on the ground that you were now walking across?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was sticky blood on the road and parts of corpses, and at one point I trod on a hand, a severed hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was this what you described as blood still wet on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sticky.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe what the foot march was like across this ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was extraordinary. We still had the car at this point packed with people sitting on top and everything. I sent out one of my colleagues up front with a torch pointing to a t-shirt, a white t-shirt hoping that the people on the other side would see a white flag. We walked for about two miles in this procession, and then we got to some rocks across the road which was the demarcation line, if you like, the frontier, in the middle of the No Man's Land. We had to leave the car there because it was a precipice on one side and a minefield around the other, so there was nowhere we could drive. So we left the car. This was a pathetic sight because people were scrambling over these rocks, when I say "rocks", there were big boulders piled up, I mean higher than a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of people were in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody. In fact it was at the rocks that one really noticed because there were a couple of people in wheelchairs and they had to be hoiked over and the wheelchairs had to be hoiked over. My recollection is a vivid one. It is just of sort of babies being handed down to parents and teddy bears, shoes and some stuff being left. It was families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Old people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Old people, very young people, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened when you reached the Bosnian Government lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We carried on walking. Some people were so scared of the firing that they tried to shelter in, as it were, the shadow left by this precipitous slope. One young man got them all to attention and said: "Look, carry on, you can't stay here." Women were crying. We would tell them to shut up because we did not know who was in the bushes. Children were crying, you told them to shut up too. Then we carried on and we were organised into a sort of single file line, so that if we were hit by mortar there would not be too many casualties. After a few more miles, I do not know how many, suddenly we saw the first Bosnian Government soldier and he told people at the front, among whom we now were, that we could not carry on down the road because the fighting in the village was too heavy, the shelling of the village in front was too heavy. So he sent us up a track, literally a sort of goat track up the side of the mountain. I had no idea what it was called or where on earth we were, but I now know it was called Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you made your way up that mountain how was the group then carried on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we staggered up the mountain for a number of hours. Some of the old people could not make it. I gather one later died. People were by now carrying their kids and the fighting was now, thankfully, left the valley below. It was in retrospect epic; at the time simply terrifying. Then after we started coming down a slope. There was a cattle trough and people stopped there to take some water, the first for a number of hours. Then buildings and I remember someone saying: "Well, I don't know where we are but it looks to be somewhere." Then exhausted by then. A man appeared out of the darkness and said: "I am with your army. Welcome to Travnik. We have buses to take you the rest of the way." By then it was about 3 o'clock in the morning and there were indeed buses waiting, well, there was a large crowd waiting to get on the buses that were coming to and fro to take people into the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If that would be a convenient place to stop before we move on to another area?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I just want to raise one matter. Mr. Vulliamy, you are excused until tomorrow at 10 a.m. You indicated, Mr. Niemann, that this is your last policy witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The delayed translation equipment is not yet installed. I spoke with someone this afternoon over lunch and I am not sure that it is going to be installed tomorrow. I do not know how long you will need with Mr. Vulliamy or whether you even need to have that equipment before you begin with your first witness with count one I guess as I recall the list. I am merely telling you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may talk to whomever you wish to to find out further information and then decide how we will proceed tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it likely to be installed on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be from what I understand, but I will get a clearer idea now that I realise that this is your last policy witness. I thought that you had three additional ones beginning with Mr. Vulliamy, but I will talk with someone and you also talk with someone. I merely wanted to pass that on to you. As Mr. Wladimiroff has been so good to pass on things that he hears, I am passing on something I hear! We will resolve it, though, this evening. We will adjourn then until tomorrow at 10 a.m. (The court adjourned until the following day). 25
